roots.name: Phthalocyanine blue pigment
roots.description: Copper phthalocyanine (PB15), an intensely coloured, heat-stable, lightfast blue used for the cool grey-blue tones on some cases. Copper plus four phthalonitrile rings, assembled in a violent exotherm.

facts.label: Colour index
facts.value: Pigment Blue 15 (PB15)

facts.label: Form used
facts.value: PB15:3 (non-flocculating / gamma form)

roots.note: Not established: that cool grey-blue C64 cases used copper phthalocyanine, the PB15:3 gamma-form assignment, or the violent-exotherm assembly description. The PB15 identity and the phthalic-anhydride route are as sourced.

roots.name: P20 pre-hardened tool steel
roots.description: A 0.38% C, 0.9% Cr, 0.4% Mo, 0.2% V steel supplied at HRC 30-35. Because it arrives hard, the whole cavity can be machined and polished with no risk of distortion from a later heat treatment, which is why it dominated housing tooling in 1982.

facts.label: Trade names
facts.value: P20, 1.2311, NAK80 is the corrosion-resistant modern cousin

roots.note: Not established: that the case tools were made in P20 or 1.2311, the stated composition, the 0.9% chromium and 0.2% vanadium, and the 28-36 HRC delivery condition. No document identifies the steel in a C64 case tool.

roots.name: Methanol (from synthesis gas)
roots.description: Made by reacting carbon monoxide and hydrogen from natural-gas reforming, a few hundred C and 50-100 bar over a copper/zinc oxide catalyst. Formaldehyde comes from methanol oxidation over silver or iron-molybdenum catalyst.

facts.label: Synthesis gas
facts.value: from natural-gas steam reforming

facts.label: Methanol synthesis
facts.value: 200-300 C, 50-100 bar, Cu/ZnO catalyst

roots.note: The synthesis-gas route and the copper/zinc oxide catalyst are established; the 200-300 C and 50-100 bar figures are not stated by the source. The formaldehyde branch over silver or iron-molybdenum is likewise uncited.

roots.name: Breadbin case: two-piece ABS shell
roots.description: The C64 'breadbin' housing is a rear shell and a front bezel, both injection-moulded general-purpose ABS in a warm beige-brown. The rear shell carries the ventilation ribs, moulded screw bosses, connector cut-outs and the rubber feet; the bezel carries the keyboard window with its square key openings, the two knurled thumbscrews, the rainbow badge and the fine 'leather' grain. A foil-on-board RFI shield sits inside over the motherboard.
roots.note: The case is universally reported as ABS - it is the polymer that browns under UV and can be reversed with peroxide retrobright bleaching. Commodore's own 2025 C64 Ultimate copy notes the surviving tooling carries a period-correct 2-point flow pattern. The wall is 2.5-3.5 mm throughout: figures of 6-8 mm quoted for thick structural mouldings do not apply to this tool and the thin wall is why the case is prone to flow marks. Merged chem.abs.c64-case noted two-shot/multi-cavity EDM texture; surviving shell shows two separate mouldings (rear-shell + bezel), so two-shot folded here as note, not fact.

children.name: Rear shell (bottom half)
children.description: The larger of the two mouldings. It forms the base pan, the raised side walls, the wrap-over top with its row of ventilation slots, the rear and side connector cut-outs, the internal ribs that stiffen the pan, the moulded screw bosses and standoffs, and the feet pads.

facts.label: Nominal wall thickness
facts.value: 2.5-3.5 mm (uniform, texturing excluded)

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ABS, general purpose, textured

facts.label: Parting line
facts.value: along the top flange, visible as a faint seam

children.name: Ventilation slots in the top wrap
children.description: A row of moulded louvre slots in the curved top panel behind the cartridge port, letting convective air out of the case over the SID and VIC-II. They are negative features cut into the tool, not separate ribs, and because they run across a thick section they leave visible flow lines and are a classic sink-mark site. Behind them the pan is stiffened with cross-ribs tying the top panel down to the base, moulded at roughly 60% of the adjacent wall gauge so the whole panel cools and shrinks as one piece.

facts.label: Style
facts.value: through-slots, parallel to the long axis

facts.label: Function
facts.value: exhaust for the linear regulator and VIC/SID heat

facts.label: Rib gauge
facts.value: 1.5-2.1 mm against a 2.5-3.5 mm wall, about 60%

facts.label: Tooling rule of thumb
facts.value: ribs capped at about 60% of the adjacent wall thickness

children.note: Effectiveness was mediocre and reviewers of the period noted heat trapping inside; the slots are modest. Mould-flow validation in 1982 was done by filling a clear polycarbonate or unfilled-PS prototype tool and watching the flow fronts by eye or on a strobe, long before short-shot first-article reports became normal.

children.name: Moulded bosses and standoffs
children.description: Integral cylindrical bosses on the pan floor that carry the four case screws, the motherboard mounting screws, the keyboard PCB screws and the RF shield tabs. Each is a thick section relative to the 3 mm pan, so the tool must be cored to keep them from sinking, and each has a blind hole with a drafted self-tapping thread. Commodore did not mould metal inserts into them; the 1982 bosses are plain ABS and it is the screw that cuts its own thread on first insertion, which is why a snapped boss rather than a rusted screw is the characteristic forty-year failure.

facts.label: Screw size
facts.value: 3 x 12 self-tapping into 6 mm OD bosses

facts.label: Boss bore
facts.value: about 2.5 mm, with a shallow helix rib

facts.label: Thread engagement
facts.value: 5-8 mm for a 3 mm screw

facts.label: Cycle to first screw-in
facts.value: about 1 s at 1200 rpm on a hand screwdriver

facts.label: Serviceability
facts.value: poor; repeated removal strips the plastic thread

children.note: Not established: the 3 x 12 screw size, the 2.5 mm bore, the 5-8 mm thread engagement and the 1200 rpm first insertion. The claim that the 1982 bosses carried no metal insert, and that a snapped boss rather than a stripped insert is the characteristic failure, is also unverified.

children.name: Rear and side connector openings
children.description: Rectangular and keyed cut-outs for the cartridge port, user port, cassette port, serial port, video DIN, power DIN and the two DE-9 control ports. Cut with knife-edged steel on the tool; the moulded lip around each port also acts as a draft and a finger stop, and the mouldings carry the connector bodies as separate inserts.
children.note: The list of apertures is established from the ASSY 250407 parts list: CN1 Header Assy, 20 Pin, 903331-20; CN4 6 Pin Din, 903361-01 (cassette); CN5 8 Pin Din, 325573-01 (video, on the later 250407-04; 5 Pin Din, 903362-01 on the earliest); CN6 44 Pin Card Edge, 906100-02 (cartridge/expansion); CN8,9 Plug Assy, 9 Pin MINI-D, 251057-01 (control ports). The cartridge port also has its own moulded guide part, Cartridge Guide 326116-01, and the power rocker and joystick apertures are listed as Connector Panel (ON, OFF, Joystick) 326299-01. Not established: the draft and finger-stop detail on the moulded lip. Note the circuit-theory text calls the later video output an eight pin connector while the 250425 parts list also carries a 7 Pin Din, CN7 251116-01, so the manual is not internally consistent on that connector.

Not established: the 2.5-3.5 mm nominal wall, the material grade and the parting-line position on the breadbin rear shell. The top and bottom case parts are documented as parts 326113-01 and 326114-01; their construction is not.

children.name: Front bezel (top half)
children.description: The dished front panel with the keyboard window. It is the visible part of the machine, so it carries the fine leather-grain texture, the rainbow badge recess, the two knurled thumbscrews and the moulded-in 'COMMODORE' lettering on the lower lip.

facts.label: Keyboard window
facts.value: 66 square openings on about 14 mm pitch

facts.label: Texture
facts.value: fine stochastic leather/pebble grain, 0.05-0.15 mm deep, cut by EDM

facts.label: Screws to rear shell
facts.value: 6 self-tapping, plus 2 at the rear lip

children.name: Keyboard window and key openings
children.description: A single rectangular opening spanned by thin webs between the key holes; the caps push through and their plungers sit on the keyboard PCB below. The webs are the highest-risk area of the tool for short shots and flash, because the melt has to snake between 66 holes that are only about 10 mm across.

facts.label: Web width
facts.value: 2-3 mm between adjacent holes

facts.label: Flash tolerance
facts.value: <0.2 mm, visually rejected at final inspection

children.note: Whether the bezel was a single moulding with the key openings, or a bezel with a separate keyboard frame, varies between breadbin tooling generations. Photographs of ASSY 250407 show one piece. The webs between the openings are the highest-risk area of the tool for short shots and flash, because the melt has to snake between sixty-six holes of only about 10 mm across.

children.name: Knurled thumbscrews for contrast/brightness
children.description: Two moulded plastic thumbscrews on the bezel that carry small metal shafts to the contrast and brightness potentiometers on the board. The caps are ABS, the shafts are plated steel, and the knurl is moulded rather than cut.
children.note: On some breadbin boards the potentiometers were adjusted by reaching into the case with a screwdriver and the two bezel thumbscrews only appear on later board revisions; check the specific assembly.

children.name: Rainbow Commodore badge
children.description: The rainbow Commodore badge on the bezel: a shallow raised island, moulded as part of the bezel tool so that it is smooth while the surrounding case carries the leather grain, and printed with coloured and metallised pad-print ink. The ink is the badge; the ABS of the bezel is only the substrate it sits on, which is why the badge has no resin ingredient of its own. Later machines carry the same mark as a flat printed decal applied at the factory rather than as part of the shell.
children.note: An input reading "ABS bezel surface" used to resolve to the case resin, which asserted the badge was made of ABS. It is not: it is a film of ink 10-30 um thick on a raised pad of the same ABS. Corrected here to point at the inks. Replicas, second-hand cases and modern reproductions disagree about whether the badge is raised mould or a bonded medallion; surviving originals show a raised pad-printed area with the ink sitting in the texture, which is the most likely reading.

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: raised untextured island in the bezel mould, same ABS

facts.label: Decoration
facts.value: pad-printed colour plus metallised aluminium flake in the bright bars

facts.label: Ink film
facts.value: of the order of 10-30 um

facts.label: Later machines
facts.value: flat printed decal rather than part of the shell

children.note: Not established: the 66 openings and their pitch, the grain depth and pitch, and the screw count on the C64 front bezel. The bezel is the Top Case, Commodore part 326113-01, and the case screws are listed as self-tapping.

children.name: Case feet
children.description: Four small anti-vibration feet on the underside of the bottom case that stop the machine skating on a desk and stop the ABS case from ringing against it. Commodore's own parts documentation lists them as self-adhesive stick-on feet, separate from the case, rather than as elastomer moulded into the shell.

facts.label: Fixing
facts.value: self-adhesive, stuck to the bottom case; not moulded into the shell

facts.label: Compound
facts.value: a soft dark elastomer; the service manual names no material

children.note: The mounting method was wrong until the service manual was consulted. Its parts lists for the C64 bottom case assembly and the C64C bottom case both describe the foot as "Foot, Self-Adhesive", i.e. a stick-on pad applied to the case, which contradicts the insert-moulded or pressed-in reading this node previously carried and vindicates the common restorer's replacement with stick-on silicone bumpers: the originals were already adhesive pads. What the manual does not give is the compound, so the styrene-butadiene and soft PVC guesses here are unsupported, and the foot's behaviour in service is not described anywhere. Confidence stays medium because the compound and the age of the adhesive are unestablished.

children.name: RFI shield: aluminium foil on a board spacer
children.description: The C64 needed a conductive screen over the motherboard because a 1 MHz machine with a video oscillator radiates through a plastic case. Commodore used a die-cut sandwich of aluminium foil laminated to a cardboard or plastic-fibre spacer, bent into a box and stapled or taped to plastic standoffs, rather than a full metal can.

facts.label: Foil thickness
facts.value: 0.03-0.06 mm household-grade aluminium foil

facts.label: Spacer
facts.value: thin cardboard / greyboard, sometimes a plastic-fibre core

facts.label: Attachment
facts.value: stapled or taped to moulded plastic standoffs on the case floor

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: reduce RF radiation and ingress without a metal chassis

children.note: Retroleum catalogues three distinct breadbin foil-shield types (Types 1, 2 and 5) which tells you the shape was not standardised across the production run. Later boards (250425) got a stamped metal shield/heatsink that doubled as a cooler for the linear regulators.

children.name: Case fasteners
children.description: The screws that hold the C64 together: a handful of case-assembly screws plus the motherboard and keyboard mounting screws. They are cheap zinc-plated self-tapping screws driven into plain plastic bosses. The wire arrives as EBSD or BQ grade, is drawn, cut to length and cold-headed on a multiple-spindle header that makes tens of thousands an hour, then plated: 5-15 um of zinc from an acid or alkaline bath, usually with a yellow or clear chromate conversion coat for corrosion resistance. Zinc is chosen because it is sacrificial and cheap.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: cold-drawn carbon steel, EBSD/BQ wire drawn to about 2 mm

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: 5-15 um zinc, chromate-passivated

facts.label: Thread-forming
facts.value: self-tapping plastics thread, 3 x 12 typical

facts.label: Header output
facts.value: tens of thousands of screws an hour, essentially no machining

facts.label: Common failure
facts.value: a stripped ABS boss, not a rusted screw

children.note: Rolled threads are stronger than cut ones, but on a 3 mm screw of this class the distinction barely matters next to the boss. Repro cases now mould brass inserts into the boss to fix exactly this failure.

children.name: Moulded-in brass insert (later practice)
children.description: Modern repro cases and late Commodore tools mould a brass or stainless insert into the boss and use a real machine screw. The insert is placed by hand or by gravity feed and captured by the ABS on the next shot, giving a reusable metal thread.

facts.label: Insert material
facts.value: brass (Cu-Zn) or stainless

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: serviceable thread, no boss breakage

children.note: Original 1982 breadbins used self-tapping screws into plain plastic bosses. Inserts are the later improvement, and are the reason a repro case does not break at the boss the way the original does.

facts.label: Nominal wall thickness
facts.value: 2.5-3.5 mm, uniform, texturing excluded

facts.label: Case screws
facts.value: 3 x 12 self-tapping zinc-plated, into moulded bosses

facts.label: Shells
facts.value: rear shell and front bezel, both general-purpose ABS

facts.label: Colour
facts.value: pigmented in the resin at compounding, never sprayed

roots.name: Keyboard module: 66 keycaps on hybrid switches
roots.description: The C64's keyboard is a separate wired module that drops into the bezel: a steel backplate, a single-sided printed circuit board carrying the matrix, sixty-six individually moulded ABS keycaps, and beneath each cap a rubber-dome switch - a moulded plunger riding on a return spring and pressing a carbon-loaded rubber dome that bridges two plated pads on the board. The board is rigid: there is no printed flexible membrane and no silver-ink conductor anywhere in the C64 keyboard, and the only conductive element in the switch is the carbon-filled rubber itself. The legends are printed onto the cap tops with a two-colour pad printer.

facts.label: Keys
facts.value: 66 total: 2 cursor-control keys, 4 function keys, 2 SHIFT, plus the alphanumerics and named keys

facts.label: Scanned matrix
facts.value: 8 x 8 = 64 positions, read by CIA 1

facts.label: Off-matrix keys
facts.value: RESTORE on a dedicated NMI line, and SHIFT LOCK sharing the left-shift lines

facts.label: Switch construction
facts.value: carbon-loaded rubber dome on a rigid single-sided PCB; not a printed flex membrane

facts.label: Legend route
facts.value: two-colour pad printing, not double-shot moulding

facts.label: Keyboard connector
facts.value: 20-pin header at CN1 on the mainboard, front-left edge

roots.note: The service manual states KEYS 66 Keys total. The 8x8 matrix covers 64 positions; RESTORE bypasses the matrix entirely, because it drives the non-maskable interrupt, and SHIFT LOCK is a latching key wired to the same lines as the left SHIFT, so to the machine it is indistinguishable from pressing left SHIFT. Counted at 63 rather than 66 in several secondary teardowns, which is a count of matrix domes plus the cursor keys and not of the keys a user presses.

children.name: Keycaps (66 individual moulded ABS caps)
children.description: Not a single dished sheet: 66 separate rectangular caps, each moulded in dark brown-grey ABS with a slightly concave top, each dropping through its own square opening in the bezel onto its own plunger. Some breadbin sets had tan-coloured function keys, others grey.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ABS, textured, moulded one shot

facts.label: Fitting
facts.value: cross-point: ~5 mm on early breadbin caps, ~3 mm on later ones

facts.label: Legend
facts.value: printed on the top face; later sets also on the front face

facts.label: Colour variation
facts.value: function keys tan on some sets, grey on others

children.note: The count of 66 is established twice over: The C64 Keyboard has 66 keys on it, and the service manual specification lists 66 Keys total, 2 Cursor control keys and 4 Function keys. That the caps are individual moulded pieces and are not interchangeable between early and late sets is established: the 2u Return key and the 1.5u Function, Restore and Shift keys only have one female socket, which makes the keycaps non-interchangeable with newer versions of the C64 keycaps. The keyboard is a single Commodore part, 326165-02. Not established: that the caps are dark brown-grey ABS, the slightly concave top, the square openings and pitch in the bezel, that the legends are pad printed in two colours, that some later sets also print shifted characters on the front face, and the 5 mm versus 3 mm cross-point dimensions.

children.name: Keycap colour: no coding on the breadbin keyboard
children.description: Breadbin C64 caps are almost uniformly a dark brown-grey, with the function keys sometimes a lighter grey or tan. There is no per-number colour coding on the breadbin keyboard - that belongs to some other machines, and the VIC-20 had differently coloured function keys. What a C64 keycap has is a moulded-in colour, not a printed one, so the keycap colour is pigment in the ABS rather than a decoration applied afterwards.

facts.label: Number-key coding
facts.value: none on the breadbin; legends are all one colour on the cap

children.note: No colour-coded number row or overlay could be confirmed for the 1982 breadbin. Where a legend colour differs between sets it tracks the cap colour, not the key function. Treat any claim of printed colour-coded number overlays as unverified for this machine.

children.name: Cross-point fitting and cap underside
children.description: The underside of the cap carries a moulded cross that clips onto the matching cross-post on the plunger - about 5 mm on early breadbin caps, about 3 mm on later ones. The two are not interchangeable. The underside also has guide ribs that keep the cap square as it travels.

facts.label: Cross length
facts.value: ~5 mm (early breadbin) vs ~3 mm (later)

facts.label: Material
facts.value: moulded with the cap, same ABS

children.note: In part in conflict: that early and late caps are not interchangeable is established, and the difference is described as 0.25 mm in the material thickness of the cross part of the peg tops. The 5 mm and 3 mm cross lengths are not established by any source read for this node. The underside guide ribs are described by teardowns but not dimensioned.

children.name: Hybrid switches (Mitsumi-style plunger, rubber dome, spring)
children.description: The C64 does not use a rubber-dome-only membrane like a calculator, nor a mechanical switch like a typewriter. It uses a dome-and-plunger hybrid: a moulded plastic plunger carrying or driving a carbon-loaded rubber pad which bridges two plated pads on the rigid keyboard board when the cap is pressed, with a coil return spring under most keys. That gives a real click, a light touch and a definite bottom-out, which is why a C64 keyboard still feels mechanical in the 1980s sense. The rigid board is the point: there is no flexible membrane and no silver-ink trace layer in this keyboard.

facts.label: Force
facts.value: roughly 55-70 gf at the snap peak for a typical dome-and-plunger switch

facts.label: Travel
facts.value: about 3-4 mm total, of which about 0.5 mm is pre-travel

facts.label: Life
facts.value: 10-30 million operations

facts.label: Conductor
facts.value: carbon-loaded rubber; there is no silver-ink layer

children.note: That the key switches are dome-and-plunger hybrids on a rigid board rather than a membrane is established: the domes function for activating the keys, the activation pads sit on the keyboard's PCB, and the PCB is merely a collection of switches with no electronics of its own. That springs are present on the later keyboards and absent on the earliest is established: the biggest difference is the lack of springs underneath the keycaps on the early keyboard, whose domed rubber feet make it feel sluggish. Not established: the 55-70 gf snap peak, the 3-4 mm travel and 0.5 mm pre-travel, the 10-30 million operation life, and the Type 1 versus Type 2 four-pronged plunger taxonomy. The board material and the copper and gold plating processes belong to the PCB subsystem.

children.name: Switch plunger (moulded, with conductive rubber)
children.description: A small moulded body with a cross-post on top that the keycap clips onto, one or more arms that carry a conductive rubber pad, and a stem that slides in the keyboard body. Type 2 plungers have four prongs and carry a loose grey 'bubble' contact.

facts.label: Type 1
facts.value: black plungers, springs under every key, metal contact

facts.label: Type 2
facts.value: white four-pronged plungers, grey rubber bubble contacts, spring under the space bar only

children.note: That the plungers differ between generations and that the caps will not move between them is established: the plastic pegs are white and not black as in the later C64 keyboard versions, and the shape of the early keyboard's plastic pegs also differs from later ones. Not established: the four-pronged Type 2 geometry, the loose grey bubble contact, and the POM or filled nylon material.

children.name: Return spring (music wire)
children.description: A small coil spring under each key that returns the plunger. It is drawn from music wire (a high-carbon, low-carbon-content steel with a tight tensile range) and wound on a automatic spring coiler. Type 1 keyboards spring every key; Type 2 springs only the space bar and relies on the rubber dome elsewhere.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: music wire, ~0.3-0.4 mm diameter

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: set so the snap peak lands at 55-70 gf

children.note: That a coil return spring sits under each key on the later keyboards, and that the earliest keyboard has none, is established: the biggest difference is the lack of springs underneath the keycaps. Re-tensioning the keyboard key springs is a standard remedy in the repair literature. Not established: that the wire is music wire, the 0.3-0.4 mm diameter, the rate, or that Type 2 springs only the space bar.

children.name: The snap: force-displacement curve of the switch
children.description: The feel of a C64 key is a curve, not a number. The plunger rides down the spring, then the rubber dome on the board has to collapse, producing a peak in force; past the peak the force drops as the dome flattens, then rises again into the bottom-out. The peak-to-valley difference is what the finger reads as clicky, and it is the collapse of the dome rather than any metal leaf that produces it.

facts.label: Peak force
facts.value: about 55-70 gf

facts.label: Valley force
facts.value: about 25-45 gf

facts.label: Total travel
facts.value: about 3-4 mm

facts.label: Bottom-out force
facts.value: about 80-120 gf

children.note: Typical figures for dome-and-plunger switches of this period, not measured C64 data. C64 keys are famous for a light, crisp action, and the rubber dome collapsing is what gives that characteristic. The figures are recorded as facts because they are the only quantitative handle available on the feel.

children.name: Steel backplate
children.description: A sheet-steel plate under the printed circuit board with openings punched for each plunger and rolled stiffening beads pressed into it. It carries the return springs, holds the plungers' travel against the board, and is screwed to the keyboard body with about twenty small gold-coloured screws. The openings are pierced on a punch press in a single stroke across the whole sheet and the beads roll-formed afterwards: a high-volume sheet-metal job, where a tonne of steel punched this way costs a fraction of a machined equivalent.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: mild steel sheet, about 1-1.5 mm

facts.label: Openings
facts.value: punched (pierced) in one stroke for each plunger

facts.label: Piercing rate
facts.value: hundreds of strokes per minute

facts.label: Stiffening beads
facts.value: roll-formed after piercing

children.note: Not established: that the C64 keyboard has a steel backplate, its sheet thickness, and that the openings were pierced in one stroke with roll-formed stiffening beads. The plate appears in enthusiast teardowns; the press route and dimensions are not recorded.

children.name: Keyboard body and its fasteners
children.description: A moulded ABS body that holds the plungers, the PCB and the backplate, and carries the cable. It is retained by about twenty small gold-coloured screws, and on the shift-lock position it has a black-backed keyswitch with one wire running diagonally to the PCB.

facts.label: Retaining screws
facts.value: ~20 small gold-coloured screws

facts.label: Shift lock
facts.value: black-backed keyswitch, one wire runs diagonally to the PCB

children.note: That the keyboard is a separable assembly is established: it is listed as its own Commodore part, Keyboard 326165-02, under TOP CASE ASSY alongside Top Case 326113-01, Bottom Case 326114-01, LED Plate 326160-01 and Nameplate 326161-01. Not established: that the body is ABS, that about twenty small gold-coloured screws hold it together, and that the shift-lock position has one wire running diagonally to the PCB. The early keyboard's shift-lock key is described as having a black round bottom and being connected with two long yellow wires to the keyboard PCB, with most subsequent Commodore 64 keyboards having short wires, which does not match the single diagonal wire claimed here. The service manual's own two scans disagree on the keyboard part number, 326165-02 in the 1992 edition and 326166-02 in the earlier printing.

children.name: Shift-lock keyswitch
children.description: The shift-lock position carries a tiny mechanically latching slide switch: a black plastic body with a metal leaf contact that holds itself in the shifted position until pressed again. It is not a matrix key at all - it is a separate latch that simply closes the shift lines, which is why the firmware cannot tell it from a held SHIFT. On teardown it reads as a black-backed keyswitch with one wire soldered diagonally across the board.
children.note: Retroleum describes the shift-lock device as a black-backed keyswitch with one wire running diagonally to the PCB. A documented teardown with disassembly photographs finds a discrete Mitsumi latching switch plate-mounted into the keyboard PCB with a cruciform slider adapter, neither the Mitsumi standard mechanical lock nor a membrane lock; the latching-dome reading previously recorded under c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock is withdrawn for the 1982 breadbin. The later C64C revision uses a Mitsumi standard mechanical latching switch, a different part.

children.name: Keyboard retaining screws (gold-coloured)
children.description: Roughly twenty small self-tapping screws with a gold or brass finish hold the keyboard backplate and body together. The gold colour is a zinc-nickel or brass-look plating, chosen because it reads as 'quality' on a part the customer never sees.

facts.label: Finish
facts.value: gold-ish zinc-nickel or brass plating

children.note: Not established: the count, the thread and the plating on the keyboard retaining screws. The screws are visible in teardowns but no document records their specification or finish.

roots.name: Supplied cables: RF lead, A/V lead, mains cord
roots.description: Three cables shipped with or sold alongside a breadbin C64, plus the optional TV switch box. The RF cable carries the modulator's VHF output from the machine's phono socket to a television's aerial input, so it is a 75-ohm coaxial. The A/V lead carries luma, chroma, composite and audio to a monitor through an 8-pin DIN. The mains cord is a two- or three-core PVC-jacketed cord with a moulded plug that feeds the external power supply.

facts.label: RF cable
facts.value: Commodore part 326189-01, 75-ohm coax, phono to TV aerial plug

facts.label: A/V socket
facts.value: 8-pin DIN at CN5 on the motherboard; 5-pin on early sets

facts.label: Switch box
facts.value: Commodore part 904778-01, an RF splitter accessory

roots.note: The breadbin's RF modulator sits on the motherboard (Astec or Mitsumi depending on production run) and its output leaves through the machine's own phono socket. The supplied RF cable is therefore a coax lead with a phono plug at the C64 end and a television-plug at the TV end. Early boards used a 5-pin video socket; later ones an 8-pin DIN, which changes the A/V cable but not the RF cable.

children.name: RF cable (phono plug to TV plug)
children.description: A 75-ohm coaxial lead. Its job is to get a 1 MHz video signal, sitting on a VHF carrier, into a television's analogue aerial input without picking up half the room on the way. Impedance matching and a decent screen are what keep the picture from ghosting.

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm

facts.label: C64 end
facts.value: moulded phono (RCA) plug

facts.label: TV end
facts.value: coaxial television plug (the old round type)

children.note: That a 75-ohm shielded coaxial lead was a shipped accessory is established: the service manual lists RF Cable, Commodore part 326189-01, in the accessories. The structure of coax is established in general terms. Not established: that this lead ran from a moulded phono plug at the computer to a coaxial television plug, its length, or that it was bundled with the monitor rather than sold with the computer.

children.name: 75-ohm coaxial cable
children.description: The cable itself: a centre conductor, a dielectric, a braided screen and an outer PVC jacket, assembled in that order. The braid is what does the shielding; the jacket is only there to survive being dragged under a TV cabinet for twenty years. A consumer lead of this type was often thin-wall 75-ohm coax rather than a strict RG designation, and the important properties are 75 ohms and full-coverage screen.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: solid or stranded centre conductor, PE or PTFE dielectric, braided tinned-copper screen, PVC jacket

facts.label: Typical class
facts.value: RG-59 / RG-6 style 75 ohm

children.note: A 70%-covered braid leaks RF, and that leakage is why a badly-made RF cable puts a visible ghost on the picture. Anything not fully shielded is worth replacing rather than adjusting.

children.name: Braided screen (tinned copper)
children.description: A flat bundle of tinned copper wires woven over the dielectric by a braiding machine, usually with a second pass to push coverage from ~70% toward 90%. Tinning reduces oxidation and makes the braid easier to terminate.

facts.label: Coverage
facts.value: ~70-95%; more passes = better shield

facts.label: Machine
facts.value: maypole (flat) or tubular braider

children.note: That a woven copper braid serves as the concentric conducting shield in coaxial cable is established. Not established: that this braid was tinned, the 70-95% coverage figures, the second pass, and the maypole versus tubular braider. Coverage is the number that matters: a 70%-covered braid leaks RF, and that leakage is why a badly-made RF cable puts a visible ghost on the picture.

children.name: Moulded phono plug and TV plug
children.simple_name: Moulded phono plug and TV plug
children.description: Both ends are moulded: a phono (RCA) plug with a nickel-plated centre pin in a moulded barrel at the C64 end, and a television coaxial plug at the other. The pin is electroplated rather than bare so it survives being shoved into and out of the television a thousand times; nickel is the classic choice for a connector contact because its contact resistance stays low and it does not corrode in a socket. Brass is the standard pin material because it machines well, springs enough to take a wipe and does not rust.

facts.label: Phono pin
facts.value: nickel-plated brass, about 3 mm

facts.label: Barrel
facts.value: knurled, pressed or screwed onto the jacket

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: sulfate or sulfamate nickel with a brightening additive, 2-10 um

children.note: Not established: the pin material and plating, the barrel construction and the plating thickness on the C64 RF lead.

children.name: Strain-relief boot
children.description: A moulded rubber or PVC boot at each cable end where it enters the plug body, taking the bending load so the conductor does not fatigue at the termination. Cheap to add, and the difference between a lead that survives ten years and one that breaks at the root.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: PVC or vulcanised rubber

facts.label: Form
facts.value: moulded-in taper or a slid-on sleeve

children.note: Not established: that the C64 RF lead had moulded strain-relief boots at both ends, and their form.

children.name: A/V cable to a 1701/1702 monitor
children.description: A monitor lead carrying luma, chroma, composite video, audio in and out, and +5V/ground, in an 8-pin DIN connector at each end. It was often bundled with the monitor rather than sold with the computer, which is why many C64 owners improvised with a phono lead for composite only.

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: 8-pin DIN (CN5); early machines used a 5-pin socket

facts.label: Signals
facts.value: luma, chroma, composite, audio out, audio in, +5 V, ground

children.name: DIN connector and cable
children.description: A moulded DIN plug with a metal shell and a screw-on or clip-on backshell that clamps the cable and provides strain relief. The shell is nickel-plated steel or brass, and the interior is filled with a phenolic or thermoplastic insert holding the female contacts.

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: nickel-plated steel or brass

facts.label: Insert
facts.value: phenolic or thermoplastic, holding the contacts

children.note: DIN connectors on this machine are established from the parts lists: CN4 6 Pin Din 903361-01, and on the later 250407-04 CN5 8 Pin Din 325573-01, against CN5 5 Pin Din 903362-01 on the earliest. Not established: that the shell is nickel-plated steel or brass, that the insert is phenolic or thermoplastic, or that the C64's monitor ecosystem was deliberately European. The DIN plug is a European standard (DIN 41512) and is one of the few connectors where the C64's whole monitor ecosystem was deliberately European.

children.name: Cable conductors and insulation
children.description: Stranded tinned copper conductors with PVC insulation, colour-coded to the DIN pinout, with the audio lines twisted or shielded to keep the 1 MHz clock out of the speaker. The wire gauge is not recorded in the sources available here.
children.note: Not established: the conductor gauge, strand count, and jacket compound of the 1982 AV cable; the stranded tinned-copper and PVC construction is as described but no source here gives dimensions.
The monitor lead was often bundled with the monitor rather than sold with the computer, which is why many C64 owners improvised with a phono lead for composite only.

children.name: Mains power cord
children.description: A detachable mains lead for the external power supply: two or three PVC-insulated copper conductors, twisted together on a planetary twister so the cord resists unwinding, then jacketed in a second extrusion over the twisted bundle. Each conductor is passed through a die and coated with rigid or semi-rigid PVC at a few hundred volts' worth of insulation, with the colour added by pigment masterbatch. At the supply end there is a moulded figure-8 or IEC C8 inlet; at the wall end a moulded mains plug whose cord body is the part that actually fails, because it is unbolted from the prongs and slides off the cable.

facts.label: Conductors
facts.value: 2 (continental Europe) or 3 (North America, with earth)

facts.label: Insulation
facts.value: PVC per conductor, about 0.6-0.8 mm wall; line speed tens of m/min

facts.label: Outer jacket
facts.value: flexible PVC, about 2.5-3 mm wall

facts.label: Cord twist
facts.value: planetary or bunch twisting, tens of twists per metre

facts.label: Stranding
facts.value: class 2 or 5 flexible, 0.5-0.75 mm2

facts.label: Current rating
facts.value: 2.5-10 A, well over the C64's about 15 W draw

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: figure-8 (C7) or IEC C8 inlet on the power supply

children.name: Moulded mains plug
children.description: A plug with a thermoplastic cord body wrapped around the cable entry to take the bending strain, and two or three brass prongs riveted or crimped in. The cord body is the part that actually fails: the plug is unbolted from the prongs and slides off the cable.

facts.label: Prongs
facts.value: brass, plated; nickel-plated as well on the North American 3-pin plug

facts.label: Cord body
facts.value: PVC or polypropylene overmoulded grip

facts.label: Failure mode
facts.value: the cord body tears at its root after years of being yanked from the wall

children.note: Not established: the prong material and plating, the cord body polymer and the rating on the plug Commodore shipped.

Not established: the conductor count, the insulation wall, the twist rate, the stranding class and the current rating of the C64 mains lead. The service manual lists a detachable power supply but does not specify the cord. The shipped-accessories list is Users Manual, Power Supply, RF Cable and Switch Box, with the power supply a single part, 251053-02, so a detachable lead is not recorded as an accessory in its own right.

children.name: TV RF switch box
children.description: Commodore part 904778-01, an external box that let the C64's RF output share a television aerial socket with a real antenna, switching between them. It is an accessory rather than a cable, but it is the same moulded-plastic-and-coax family and shares the cable supply chain.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: switch between computer RF and TV aerial

children.note: The service-manual parts list gives this number; its exact internals are not documented in the sources available here, so the internal switch and connectors are described generically rather than specifically.

c64.case.tooling.machining.name: Machining of the cavity and core
c64.case.tooling.machining.description: A 1982 tool shop would rough the cavity with large carbide or HSS milling cutters, leaving 0.3-0.5 mm, then finish-mill, then grind the critical faces flat and parallel to 0.01-0.02 mm across the plate. The parting plane is lapped to the same figure and put exactly at the joint line of the two halves, so the flash line around the case seam disappears into the seam. Only after that does the texture go in, because the texture electrode has to follow a cavity that is already dimensionally correct.

facts.label: Plate flatness after grinding
facts.value: 0.01-0.02 mm across the plate

facts.label: Parting line
facts.value: lapped, and placed on the case joint line

facts.label: Finish target before plating
facts.value: Ra 0.2-0.4 um on polished faces

c64.case.tooling.machining.note: Not established: the stock allowance, the grinding figures, the parting-plane position and the finishing roughness on a 1982 Commodore case tool.

children.name: EDM cutting of the leather grain
children.description: The texture is the one feature of the case that cannot be milled: a random stochastic pattern of overlapping spherical dimples, 0.3-0.8 mm pitch and 0.05-0.15 mm deep. It is cut by sinking a shaped graphite or brass electrode into the hardened, ground cavity, or by wire-EDM scanning. Sinking EDM gives a whole panel at once and was well established by 1982, having been commercial since the 1960s; wire EDM gives resolution but is slower. What has not changed is that the texture is a negative in the steel and not a coating: on parts made in a second colour it can be partly buried, which is why grey aftermarket cases look so much cleaner than originals.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: sinker EDM standard for area texturing; wire EDM for detail

facts.label: Electrode
facts.value: graphite, or brass where the texture has fine features

facts.label: Rough cut
facts.value: about 0.2-0.5 mm/s removal; the finish cut is much slower

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: hydrocarbon oil (kerosene) or a synthetic dielectric

children.note: The general mechanism is documented: material is removed from the work piece by a series of rapidly recurring current discharges between two electrodes, separated by a dielectric liquid and subject to an electric voltage. Not established: the 0.3-0.8 mm grain pitch, the 0.05-0.15 mm depth, the 0.2-0.5 mm/s rough-cut rate, the kerosene dielectric, and the switch from graphite to brass for fine features. Where the texture has fine features the electrode is switched from graphite to brass, which machines more accurately but wears faster. Neither is a coating: the grain is cut into the tool steel and is reproduced on every shot the tool makes, for the life of the tool.

c64.case.tooling.polishing.name: Lapping and polishing the cavity
c64.case.tooling.polishing.description: The cavity is progressively polished - progressively finer abrasives on cloth and stone - to a mirror. On a textured tool the polish is done to the whole surface and the texture simply stays; on flat surfaces it goes to Ra 0.05-0.1 um, which is what makes the plated ABS read as glossy.

facts.label: Final flat-surface finish
facts.value: Ra 0.05-0.1 um before plating

facts.label: Polishing media
facts.value: aluminium oxide, then chromium oxide for the final mirror

facts.label: Hand vs machine
facts.value: hand polishing on cast iron blocks for the final mirror; machine polish for bulk stock removal

c64.case.tooling.polishing.note: Not established: the finished roughness figures, the media sequence and the hand-versus-machine split on a Commodore case cavity.

c64.case.tooling.plating.name: Hard chrome plating of the cavity
c64.case.tooling.plating.description: The polished cavity is electroplated in a hexavalent chromium bath to a few microns. Chrome is much harder than the tool steel, so the tool wears far better; it is also what gives the moulded ABS its character - the gloss of a C64 case is the gloss of chrome, not of steel.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: chromic acid with sulfate catalyst, 50-60 C, 6-10 V

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 3-8 um for a mould cavity

facts.label: Hydrogen embrittlement
facts.value: a real risk; many moulds are baked immediately after plating

facts.label: Why
facts.value: chrome is harder than the tool steel, and its gloss is the gloss of the moulded part

c64.case.tooling.plating.note: Hard chromium plating out of a hexavalent chromic acid bath is established. Not established: the 50-60 C bath temperature, the 6-10 V, the 3-8 um cavity thickness, and the practice of baking moulds straight after plating against hydrogen embrittlement. Modern practice has largely moved away from hexavalent chromium for environmental reasons, toward electroless nickel or PVD. In 1982 hard chrome was the standard and there was no practical alternative.

c64.packaging.wood-chips.name: Wood chips from sawmill waste
c64.packaging.wood-chips.description: Roundwood is debarked and chipped into 20-30 mm chips in a disc chipper, ready for the digester. The chips are the whole reason the paper mill sits next to a forest: you cannot make paper without wood fibre.
c64.packaging.wood-chips.note: Not established: the chipper type, the chip size and that sawmill waste was the source.

c64.packaging.log.name: Roundwood logs
c64.packaging.log.description: Trunk sections felled and delimbed, usually conifer in northern Europe and North America. Softwood is preferred for kraft because its long fibres give paper strength; hardwoods go into hardwood kraft or into mechanical pulp.
c64.packaging.log.note: Not established: the species mix, the origin and the logging route for the fibre.

c64.packaging.forest-stand.name: Standing softwood in a managed plantation
c64.packaging.forest-stand.description: Managed conifer plantations - spruce, pine or southern pine - felled on a rotation and replanted, where the fibre chain for a box begins. A box is wood, and the wood is a tree that was grown, cut and chipped.
c64.packaging.forest-stand.note: Not established: the species, the rotation length or the plantation source of the fibre.

c64.case.abs-resin.phthalic-anhydride.name: Phthalic anhydride
c64.case.abs-resin.phthalic-anhydride.description: Made by air oxidation of o-xylene over vanadia-titania catalysts at ~450 C. It is the classic route to phthalocyanine pigments and to glycidyl ester epoxy resins.

facts.label: Reactor
facts.value: fixed-bed or fluidised-bed, 400-460 C

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: vanadia-titania

c64.case.abs-resin.phthalic-anhydride.note: Partly established, and in part in conflict: the source gives vanadium pentoxide as the catalyst, not vanadia-titania, and puts the o-xylene oxidation at about 320-400 C, not the 400-460 C and ~450 C quoted here. The reactor type is not stated by the source at all.

c64.case.abs-resin.o-xylene.name: o-Xylene
c64.case.abs-resin.o-xylene.description: One of the three xylene isomers separated out of the mixed aromatics from the reformer by adsorption (UOP Parex-type) or by distillation. The ortho isomer is the one that gets oxidised to phthalic anhydride.
c64.case.abs-resin.o-xylene.note: The o-xylene to phthalic anhydride step is established; the separation route is not. The source describes o-xylene as produced by cracking petroleum, which affords a distribution of aromatic compounds including the xylene isomers, with m-xylene isomerized to o-xylene, and does not describe an adsorption unit separating the isomers. A Parex-type unit is understood to adsorb the para isomer and leave the ortho and meta isomers behind, so it does not by itself isolate o-xylene.

c64.decor.prepress.film-base.name: Film base (cellulose triacetate or polyester)
c64.decor.prepress.film-base.description: A flexible transparent film on which the emulsion is cast. Cellulose triacetate was the standard photographic film base, made from acetic anhydride and cellulose; polyester (PET) film base became common later for its dimensional stability.
c64.decor.prepress.film-base.note: Not established: whether a 1982 Commodore legend negative was on cellulose triacetate or on polyester film, and the base thickness.

c64.decor.prepress.silver-halide.name: Silver halide emulsion
c64.decor.prepress.silver-halide.description: Silver bromide or silver iodide crystals suspended in gelatin. The silver comes from silver ore, and most photographic silver of the era was recovered as a byproduct of lead and copper refining rather than mined for itself.
c64.decor.prepress.silver-halide.note: That the light-sensitive constituent of a photographic emulsion is a silver halide is established: Daguerre redirected his efforts toward the light-sensitive silver halides, and sodium thiosulphate was found to be a solvent of silver halides and to fix silver-halide-based photographs. Not established: that the crystals here are specifically silver bromide or silver iodide suspended in gelatin, and that most photographic silver of the era was recovered as a byproduct of lead and copper refining rather than mined for itself.

c64.decor.prepress.acetic-acid.name: Acetic acid and acetic anhydride
c64.decor.prepress.acetic-acid.description: Made by catalytic oxidation of ethanol, or by the carbonylation of methanol. Methanol comes from synthesis gas, which comes from natural-gas reforming.

facts.label: Carbonylation
facts.value: methanol + CO to acetic acid, rhodium catalyst, 150-200 C

c64.decor.prepress.acetic-acid.note: The methanol carbonylation route is established and was the dominant one: rhodium-catalysed methanol carbonylation became the dominant method of acetic acid production, with the first plant on that catalyst built in 1970. Not established: the 150-200 C figure, the ethanol-oxidation alternative, and that the acetic anhydride for a cellulose triacetate base came from this route. Cellulose triacetate film base is made from acetic anhydride, which is made from methanol by carbonylation. So the negative that carries a keycap legend is partly wood and partly natural gas, which is as far as this trail usefully goes.

c64.decor.prepress.cellulose.name: Cellulose (for triacetate)
c64.decor.prepress.cellulose.description: Dissolved from wood pulp and regenerated into fibre. The film route is a small, high-purity use of cellulose compared with paper, but it is the same feedstock: a tree.
c64.decor.prepress.cellulose.note: Not established: wood pulp as the feedstock for the film used here, the dissolved-and-regenerated-into-fibre description (triacetate film is acetylated and dry-spun, not regenerated), or that the prepress negative was triacetate rather than polyester.

c64.decor.metallised.flake.name: Atomised aluminium flake
c64.decor.metallised.flake.description: Molten aluminium atomised with air into 5-15 um flakes, then washed, sieved by size and coated with an oxidation-inhibiting lacquer so they do not go grey. The same atomisation principle as the aluminium in the EMI shield, at a different scale: the flake is pigment, the foil is sheet.

facts.label: Atomisation
facts.value: air-blast or mechanical, about 1400 C melt

facts.label: Flake size
facts.value: 5-15 um, sieved

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: lacquer or chromate wash to stop further oxidation

c64.decor.metallised.flake.note: Not established: the flake size range and the passivation route on a 1982 Commodore ink. Atomised aluminium flake pigment is an old and well documented material; the specific grading applied here is not.

c64.decor.metallised.binders.name: Metallised ink binder
c64.decor.metallised.binders.description: A drying ink binder that holds the flakes flat and lets them reflect. Formulated so the flake lies parallel to the surface; this is what produces the flat metallic look rather than a sparkly one.
c64.decor.metallised.binders.note: Not established: the formulated-binder claim, that the binder holds aluminium flake parallel to the surface and produces the flat metallic look, for any specific 1982 ink; no formulation or supplier record backs it.

c64.decor.pad-print.ink-resin.name: Ink binder resin (alkyd or acrylic)
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-resin.description: The film-forming part of the ink: an alkyd built from drying-oil fatty acids and a polyacid (the same chemistry as the printing ink vehicle on the box), or an acrylic copolymer. It is chosen for adhesion to ABS, which is notoriously hard to print on without a surface treatment.
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-resin.note: ABS has a low surface energy and low surface tension (~38-39 dynes/cm, against ~72 for water), which is why printing ink on it needs a good wetting binder or a plasma/corona treatment - and why the legends on a forty-year-old cap can be abraded off but not easily peeled.

c64.decor.pad-print.ink-pigment.name: Legend and logo pigments
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-pigment.description: The legend white is almost always titanium dioxide in an alkyd binder; the rainbow logo uses a set of saturated organic pigments - phthalocyanine blue, quinacridone magenta, azo yellow - and sometimes a metallised flake for the bright bars.
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-pigment.note: Not established: which pigments were in the Commodore keycap and badge inks. The pigment supply chain converges on the same handful of chemical plants as the case masterbatch and the box ink; its use in these inks is not.

c64.decor.pad-print.ink-solvent.name: Ink solvent (glycol ether / ester blend)
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-solvent.description: The volatile carrier that gives pad ink its low viscosity. Common 1980s pad-ink solvents were propylene glycol ethers, dibutyl phthalate or xylene blends. It flashes off the pad quickly enough to give a sharp print and slowly enough that the impression can be placed.
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-solvent.note: Solvent-based pad ink is largely gone from consumer goods today because of VOC regulation; UV-curing pad ink, which needs no solvent at all, is the modern replacement and was already available in 1982.

c64.decor.pad-print.pad-compound.name: Two-part silicone pad compound
c64.decor.pad-print.pad-compound.description: A polydimethylsiloxane casting system cured at room temperature with a tin catalyst, or an addition-cure platinum system. Pads are cast in a mould against the plate image so that the relief matches the cliche exactly; the chemistry is the same PDMS as the conductive rubber in the keyboard switch and as the pad-printing pad itself.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: room temperature about 24 h, or heat-accelerated addition cure

c64.decor.pad-print.pad-compound.note: Not established: the pad compound, the tin-catalysed room-temperature cure and the 24 hour figure. Pad printing is documented to use a silicone pad; the casting chemistry is not.

c64.packaging.kraft-pulp.name: Kraft pulp
c64.packaging.kraft-pulp.description: Wood chips are steamed, cooked in a kraft digester with sodium hydroxide and sodium sulfide, washed, and bleached only lightly. The kraft cook is a delignifying cook: it removes most of the lignin originally present in the wood, and the surviving cellulose is what makes kraft pulp stronger than sulfite or mechanical pulp. Kraft pulp is darker than other wood pulps and is normally left unbleached for sack and liner grades.

facts.label: Cook
facts.value: kraft/sulfate cook at 160-180 C

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: ~45-50% of wood weight

c64.packaging.kraft-pulp.note: That kraft pulp is produced by the kraft process and that the process yields stronger pulp than sulfite or mechanical pulping is established. In part in conflict: the source says kraft pulping removes most of the lignin present originally in the wood, whereas the description here says the brown colour is retained kraft lignin. Not established: the sodium hydroxide and sodium sulfide charges, the 160-180 C cook, the one to three hour duration and the 45-50% yield.

c64.packaging.paper.name: Uncoated printing and packaging paper
c64.packaging.paper.description: A Fourdrinier sheet of matted cellulose fibre, formed from a dilute kraft-pulp slurry that is drained on a moving wire, pressed between rolls and steam-dried to about 6 percent moisture. It is the common base behind the manual pages, the warranty card and the packaging inserts: coating, sizing or a heavier board grade all start from this sheet.

facts.label: Furnish
facts.value: bleached or unbleached kraft pulp, with mechanical or recycled fibre where the grade allows

facts.label: Printing grades
facts.value: about 60-120 gsm; card above about 160 gsm

facts.label: Drying
facts.value: steam-heated cans above 93 C, sheet to about 6 percent moisture

c64.packaging.paper.note: Established: that paper is a thin sheet of matted cellulose fibre formed from a pulp slurry drained and dried into sheets; that kraft pulp makes linerboard and printing and writing papers; steam-can drying to about 6 percent moisture; clay, calcium carbonate and titanium dioxide as opacity fillers and kaolin as the coating clay. Made of rather than made from its pulp because the sheet is the same cellulose fibres in a different shape (slurry versus web), with only water removed and no chemical transformation; this follows the foil, sheet and wire precedent in the metals branches. Not established: the furnish blend, the grammage and the bleaching route of the stocks Commodore bought, or which mill made them. Recycled OCC fibre is deliberately not linked here: it feeds the corrugated medium, not printing grades.

c64.packaging.papermaking.name: Make paper on a Fourdrinier machine
c64.packaging.papermaking.description: Refined kraft pulp is blended, diluted and jetted from a headbox at under 0.4 percent consistency onto a moving wire, where vacuum drains it to about 25 percent solids at the couch. Press rolls with felts take the web above 40 percent solids, steam-heated cans dry it to about 6 percent moisture, and the reel winds it for slitting into sheets or rolls.

facts.label: Headbox consistency
facts.value: typically under 0.4 percent

facts.label: Couch solids
facts.value: about 25 percent

facts.label: Press solids
facts.value: above 40 percent

facts.label: Dryers
facts.value: steam-heated cans above 93 C, in runs of forty or more

c64.packaging.papermaking.note: Established: the forming, press and dryer sections and the headbox, couch, press and reel moisture figures. Not established: the wire width, the machine speed and whether the supplying mill ran an integrated pulp line; tissue and multi-ply board variants are not this grade.

c64.packaging.eps-beads.name: EPS beads (expanded in a bead expander)
c64.packaging.eps-beads.description: Styrene is suspension-polymerised in water to small beads, then a blowing agent is dissolved into them under pressure; on heating the agent flashes and expands each bead, and the beads are chilled and sieved by size.

facts.label: Bead size
facts.value: raw about 0.5-1 mm; expanded 2-6 mm

facts.label: Blowing agent
facts.value: pentane or another aliphatic hydrocarbon; chlorinated agents such as CFC-11 were also used. The agent in this package is not established.

facts.label: Expansion
facts.value: about 100-140 C steam at 1-2 bar

c64.packaging.eps-beads.note: Not established, and in conflict: that the blowing agent in 1982 EPS was CFC-11 or dichloromethane. Expanded polystyrene beads made with a pentane blowing agent were patented in 1949, so the chlorinated agent was not the only route and may not have been the one used here. Bead sizes and the steam conditions are also unverified.

c64.packaging.chlorinated-blowing-agent.name: Chlorinated blowing agent (CFC-11 / dichloromethane)
c64.packaging.chlorinated-blowing-agent.description: Trichlorofluoromethane, or methylene chloride in the European trade. Both are excellent blowing agents: low boiling point, no flammability risk in the bead, and chemically inert enough to survive the polymerisation. They are also chlorinated, which is the whole problem - they destroy stratospheric ozone, so they were phased out of packaging foam through the 1990s and replaced by pentane and by butane.

facts.label: Why chosen then
facts.value: non-flammable, cheap, and already produced in bulk as a refrigerant

c64.packaging.chlorinated-blowing-agent.note: Not established: that a chlorinated blowing agent was used in C64 packing foam. Both agents boiling points and the Montreal Protocol phase-out are documented chemistry; their use in this package is not recorded.

c64.packaging.kraft-liner.name: Kraft liner (topside and underside)
c64.packaging.kraft-liner.description: Unbleached paper made from long-fibre softwood pulp, typically 120-200 gsm. Kraft paper is also known as brown paper: the brown is the colour of the unbleached grade, not the consequence of a lignin-preserving cook, because the kraft cook in fact removes most of the lignin present in the wood.

facts.label: Fibre
facts.value: long-fibre softwood (spruce, pine)

c64.packaging.kraft-liner.note: In part in conflict. That unbleached kraft is the strong, cheap liner grade is established, and so is the reason it is strong: kraft pulping removes most of the lignin present originally in the wood, and the low lignin matters because the hydrophobic nature of lignin interferes with the hydrogen bonds between cellulose fibres. That is the opposite of the explanation given here, which is that the brown colour comes from the kraft cook keeping the lignin. The brown colour of kraft paper is established as the colour of the unbleached grade itself, kraft paper also being known as brown paper; the mechanism by which it is brown is not settled by the source.

c64.packaging.corrugated-medium.name: Fluted medium (recycled)
c64.packaging.corrugated-medium.description: The wavy centre of the board is usually made from 100% recycled paper, because the flute does not need virgin-fibre strength. Old corrugated boxes are collected, pulped (the recycled / OCF route), and run onto a corrugating machine.
c64.packaging.corrugated-medium.note: Not established: that the fluted medium was 100% recycled. Recycled medium is common practice but the fibre blend on this board is not recorded.

c64.packaging.starch-adhesive.name: Starch corrugating adhesive
c64.packaging.starch-adhesive.description: The glue holding the flutes and the liners is a corn- or tapioca-starch dextrin, cooked on the corrugator and applied hot. It is the standard adhesive in corrugated board and the reason the board is not a fire hazard in the way solvent glues would be.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: starch / dextrin, hot-water resistant grade for the liners

c64.packaging.corn-starch.name: Corn (maize) starch
c64.packaging.corn-starch.description: Starch is wet-milled from maize: the kernels are steeped in warm water to soften the germ, ground, and the starch is separated by gravity or centrifugally and dried. Every corrugated box is glued with a plant, not a petrochemical.
c64.packaging.corn-starch.note: Not established: that the corrugating adhesive was a maize or tapioca starch dextrin. Starch is the documented corrugating adhesive; the source crop is not recorded.

c64.packaging.maize.name: Maize crop
c64.packaging.maize.description: A cereal grain grown in enormous tonnages in the US corn belt and in Europe, China and Brazil; the harvested cobs are shelled and the kernels go to wet milling. This is the agricultural end of the adhesive chain.
c64.packaging.maize.note: Not established: any Commodore figure for maize tonnage or origin. The adhesive chain is documented to the level of plant starch.

c64.packaging.wastepaper.name: Recovered paper (OCC / mixed waste)
c64.packaging.wastepaper.description: Collected corrugated and box board, baled, repulped in a hydrapulper and screened. The deinking stage is needed for printed waste; unprinted OCC is repulped as it is. The fibre in a C64 box's fluted medium is therefore almost certainly several previous boxes.

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: OCC (old corrugated container) or mixed waste paper

facts.label: Baling
facts.value: hydraulic baler to ~500 kg bales

c64.packaging.wastepaper.note: That old corrugated containers are the characteristic post-consumer waste stream for board fibre is established: post-consumer waste is discarded after consumer use, such as old corrugated containers (OCC), magazines, and newspapers. Not established: the 500 kg bale weight, the specific grade used for C64 board, and that the fibre in this box is several previous boxes.

c64.packaging.ink-resin.name: Alkyd ink vehicle
c64.packaging.ink-resin.description: Built from vegetable oil (linseed or soybean) fatty acids condensed with a polyol and a phthalic or maleic anhydride, then crosslinked by oxidative polymerisation on the press. So the ink vehicle on the box traces back to a phthalic anhydride plant, the same chemistry as the pigment in the case.

facts.label: Vehicle
facts.value: linseed or soy alkyd resin

c64.packaging.soy-oil.name: Soy or linseed oil (ink vehicle base)
c64.packaging.soy-oil.description: A vegetable oil pressed from a crop. It oxidises (dries) on the printed sheet, which is what 'drying ink' means. In 1982 soybean oil was becoming the preferred ink vehicle because of the 1970s linseed-oil shortages.
c64.packaging.soy-oil.note: Not established: that soybean oil was the ink vehicle on C64 packaging in 1982, and that the 1970s linseed shortage drove the switch. Alkyd vehicles are documented; the crop on Commodore packaging is not.

c64.packaging.ink-pigment.name: Ink pigments (organic and inorganic)
c64.packaging.ink-pigment.description: In 1982 most packaging colourants were still inorganic: iron oxides, chrome yellow, ultramarine. The bright synthetic organic pigments (phthalocyanines, azo yellows) were used for the saturated rainbow, and the titanium dioxide white for the light areas.
c64.packaging.ink-pigment.note: Not established: the pigment set in 1982 Commodore packaging inks. The named pigments are all documented materials; their use on these boxes is not.

c64.cables.rf-cable.plasticiser.name: Plasticiser in flexible PVC
c64.cables.rf-cable.plasticiser.description: Cable PVC is not rigid: it is compounded with a plasticiser such as dioctyl phthalate (DOP) or trimellitates, dropped into an extruder at 5-10% and mixed before extrusion. The plasticiser is what makes the lead supple instead of stiff and brittle.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: 5-15% by weight

facts.label: Common plasticisers
facts.value: DOP (DEHP), DINP, trimellitate esters

c64.cables.rf-cable.plasticiser.note: Not established: that a phthalate plasticiser was used in the C64 RF cable jacket, and the loading.

c64.cables.rf-cable.ldpe.name: Low-density polyethylene (the volume dielectric)
c64.cables.rf-cable.ldpe.description: The bulk of consumer coax dielectric is LDPE made by high-pressure or low-pressure polymerisation of ethylene. LDPE is branched and low-density, which is exactly what you want here: the branching lowers the dielectric constant so the coaxial geometry lands on 75 ohm with a reasonable centre-conductor size.
c64.cables.rf-cable.ldpe.note: That LDPE is the branched low-density form of polyethylene is established: the article heads its structure section with the branched structure of LDPE, and identifies branching as one of the features that distinguishes polyethylene grades. Not established: that the branching is what allows a 75 ohm coaxial geometry with a reasonable centre conductor, the 2.2-2.35 dielectric constant and the 0.91-0.93 g/cm3 density.

c64.case.tooling.synthetic-alumina.name: Synthetic alumina abrasive
c64.case.tooling.synthetic-alumina.description: Bauxite is refined to alumina and sintered or fused into corundum, then crushed and graded into abrasive powders. Hardness ~9 on the Mohs scale, second only to diamond, and the workhorse of metal finishing.

facts.label: Fused alumina
facts.value: ~2100 C in an arc furnace

c64.case.tooling.synthetic-alumina.note: Not established: the fusion temperature and the abrasive grading applied on Commodore tooling.

c64.case.tooling.graphite-ore.name: Natural graphite flake
c64.case.tooling.graphite-ore.description: Flake graphite is mined in Sri Lanka, Madagascar, China and Brazil, purified by acid (or in the 1980s by chlorination) and pressed with pitch binder into tooling graphite.
c64.case.tooling.graphite-ore.note: Not established: the mining origins, the purification route and that China supplied Commodore tooling graphite.

c64.decor.screen-print.neoprene.name: Neoprene squeegee rubber
c64.decor.screen-print.neoprene.description: Polychloroprene, chosen because it resists the solvents in screen ink and wears well. It is the same chloroprene rubber used for cable jackets and gaskets, again pointing back to the C4 cracker cut.
c64.decor.screen-print.neoprene.note: Neoprene, also polychloroprene, is established as a family of synthetic rubbers produced by polymerisation of chloroprene, which exhibits good chemical stability and maintains flexibility over a wide temperature range. Not established: that it was chosen specifically for solvent resistance against screen inks, and the same chloroprene compound being used for cable jackets and gaskets.

c64.packaging.manual.paper.name: Coated printing paper
c64.packaging.manual.paper.description: Wood-pulp paper filled and coated with clay (kaolin) and a binder, then calendered, so the ink sits on the surface and the colours are bright and sharp. It is the same stock as a supermarket leaflet.

facts.label: Gramnage
facts.value: 60-100 gsm coated

facts.label: Coating
facts.value: kaolin/clay + starch or PVA binder

facts.label: Fibre
facts.value: mostly softwood mechanical and kraft pulp

c64.packaging.manual.paper.note: Not established: the grammage, the coating and the furnish of the stock the C64 manual was printed on.

c64.packaging.eps.name: Expanded polystyrene (EPS)
c64.packaging.eps.description: Small beads of polystyrene, each already blown up with a blowing agent, heated and expanded again in a mould so the beads fuse into a solid block shaped to the part. The polymer is the same styrene feedstock as the ABS and the SAN; only the physical form is different. The documented blowing agent is pentane, an aliphatic hydrocarbon permeating the bead before expansion; chlorinated blowing agents were also used and were being eliminated from foam through the 1980s and 1990s.

facts.label: Blowing agent
facts.value: pentane is the commonly used blowing agent, absorbed into the bead and expanded by heat and steam; chlorinated agents were earlier and were phased out of foam through the 1980s and 1990s

facts.label: Pentane-bead process
facts.value: developed before 1949 by F. Stastny and patented by BASF and Stastny in 1949; first public demonstration 1952

facts.label: Regulation
facts.value: US municipal bans on CFC foam containers began 1987, which removed CFC from foam rather than introducing pentane, the documented agent from 1949

facts.label: Which agent in this package
facts.value: not established; no Commodore document records the packing foam formulation

c64.packaging.eps.note: Corrected: this node previously stated the 1982 blowing agent was CFC-11 or dichloromethane, with pentane arriving only after the 1987 Montreal Protocol. The documented history runs the other way: pentane-blown beads were patented in 1949, and the 1987 bans removed CFC from foam rather than introducing pentane. Which agent the C64 packing foam actually used is not established; no Commodore document records the formulation.

c64.packaging.box-board.name: Corrugated board (liner + medium)
c64.packaging.box-board.description: Two kraft liners glued to a fluted medium, corrugated between two rotating fluted rolls with heat and starch glue and then glued to the liners. The flute is a beam, which is the whole reason a pizza box folds and a used sheet does not, and it is why a C64 box is B or C flute single wall rather than anything heavier. Medium paper is run onto the corrugator at 200-400 m/min and the sheet is then cut and creased.

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: liner / fluted medium / liner, single wall

facts.label: Typical flute
facts.value: B (about 2.5 mm) or C (about 4 mm)

facts.label: Adhesive
facts.value: starch or dextrin, hot-water resistant grade

facts.label: Machine speed
facts.value: about 200-400 m/min

c64.packaging.box-board.note: Reusing office paper makes poor medium; box fibre is preferred because the flute is only as strong as the paper in it.

c64.packaging.strapping.name: Strapping (steel or polypropylene)
c64.packaging.strapping.description: Steel band with a stamped seal, or the polypropylene strapping that had largely displaced it by the 1980s because it does not rust, does not cut the carton and is lighter to ship back as waste.
c64.packaging.strapping.note: Not established: whether the export cartons were banded with steel or with polypropylene, and the band specification.

c64.packaging.carton-board.name: Master-carton board
c64.packaging.carton-board.description: Heavier double-wall corrugated, usually a recycled medium and recycled liners, with the shipping marks stencilled or flexo-printed rather than litho-printed.
c64.packaging.carton-board.note: Not established: that the master carton was double-wall recycled board with stencilled marks. Single-wall construction and starch bonding of corrugated board are documented; the shipping carton specification is not.

c64.packaging.timber.name: Rough-sawn softwood
c64.packaging.timber.description: Kiln-dried or green softwood, band-sawn to bearers and deckboards. The sawmill waste that cannot be pulped into paper - knots, ends, slabs - is exactly what a skid is made of, which is a neat closure of the wood chain.

facts.label: Species
facts.value: pine, spruce or fir

facts.label: Moisture
facts.value: green or kiln-dried, depending on the shipping leg

c64.packaging.timber.note: Not established: the species, the moisture condition and the section sizes of the export skid.

c64.cables.rf-cable.centre-conductor.name: Centre conductor (copper, or copper-clad steel)
c64.cables.rf-cable.centre-conductor.description: The signal-carrying core. Consumer coax uses solid bare copper or, to save money, copper-clad steel. At RF frequencies a copper-clad-steel core is perfectly adequate over a metre of cable, and the copper wire rod for it comes from the same electrolytic refinery as the winding wire and the contact metal elsewhere in the machine.
c64.cables.rf-cable.centre-conductor.note: That the signal-carrying core of a coaxial cable is the inner centre conductor is established. Not established: that consumer coax of this period used copper-clad steel to save money, that a copper-clad-steel core is adequate over a metre at RF, or that the rod for it came from the same refinery as the machine's other conductors. Cable plants buy cathode and draw rod in-house; drawing anneals and work-hardens the copper in the same step.

c64.cables.rf-cable.dielectric.name: Dielectric (polyethylene or PTFE)
c64.cables.rf-cable.dielectric.description: The insulating foam between conductor and braid. Polyethylene is the volume material for consumer coax, often gas-injected or foam-injected to lower the dielectric constant and hold 75 ohm with a bigger centre conductor. PTFE (Teflon) is the low-loss, low-noise alternative used where a very clean signal or a tight bend radius matters.

facts.label: Volume choice
facts.value: polyethylene, often foamed

facts.label: Premium choice
facts.value: PTFE for low loss and low dielectric constant

facts.label: Extrusion
facts.value: pre-extruded dielectric tube, then conductor drawn in

c64.cables.rf-cable.dielectric.note: That the insulating material between the centre conductor and the shield is the dielectric is established. Not established: that polyethylene was the volume choice for consumer coax, that it was gas- or foam-injected, and that PTFE was the premium choice. Foamed polyethylene is worth noting because it is the same polymer as the plastic bags in the packaging: chain-grafted or chemical-blowing-agent foam, blown in the extrusion line.

c64.cables.rf-cable.jacket.name: Coaxial cable PVC jacket
c64.cables.rf-cable.jacket.description: A lead-compounded PVC jacket, flexible grade with a plasticiser so the cable stays bendable. It has nothing to do with the signal; its job is abrasion and handling. The plasticiser is what makes the lead supple instead of stiff and brittle, and the phthalate ester it is made from comes off the same phthalic anhydride plant as the pigment in the case.

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: flexible (plasticised) PVC

facts.label: Wall
facts.value: about 0.7-1.0 mm

c64.cables.rf-cable.jacket.note: Not established: the jacket grade and wall thickness on the C64 RF lead, and which plasticiser was used.

c64.cables.power-cord.conductors.name: Flexible stranded copper conductors
c64.cables.power-cord.conductors.description: Fine-strand flexible copper, made by bunching many small wires in a roving machine and twisting them. Flexible stranding is what lets a mains lead bend without breaking the strands, and class 2 or 5 stranding at 0.5-0.75 mm2 is what a 2.5-10 A cord of this period used.

facts.label: Stranding
facts.value: class 2 or 5 flexible, 0.5-0.75 mm2 conductors

facts.label: Machine
facts.value: bunching and twisting (stranding) machine

c64.cables.power-cord.conductors.note: Not established: the stranding class, the conductor cross-section and that the lead was bunched on a roving machine.

c64.cables.power-cord.cord-body.name: Cord body / strain-relief grip
c64.cables.power-cord.cord-body.description: Moulded in PVC or polypropylene and over-moulded onto the jacket. It is deliberately flexible so the cable can swivel, which is also why a moulded cord body eventually tears at its root after years of being yanked out of a wall socket by the wire.
c64.cables.power-cord.cord-body.note: Not established: the cord body polymer and whether it was overmoulded onto the jacket.

c64.keyboard.cable.conductor.name: Ribbon conductors
c64.keyboard.cable.conductor.description: Either a flat laminated ribbon of stranded copper conductors or a bundle of discrete stranded leads; the ribbon is thinner, discrete leads are more flexible at the fold. Whatever the construction, the keyboard cable is the link to the mainboard and has nothing to do with the switch matrix: the matrix lives on a rigid board inside the module.
c64.keyboard.cable.conductor.note: Whether a given C64 keyboard cable is a flat ribbon or a discrete loom is a per-run detail; both are consistent with the era and with the 20-pin connector. The material is PVC or polyester insulation over stranded copper, not a printed flexible circuit.

c64.keyboard.switches.plunger-polymer.name: Plunger polymer: acetal or filled nylon
c64.keyboard.switches.plunger-polymer.description: The plunger has to be dimensionally stable over millions of strokes and low-friction against the spring and the body.
