Acetal (POM) is the classic choice for its low friction and stiffness; glass-filled nylon or polycarbonate are also used. All three are moulded on small multi-cavity tools, and the formaldehyde and nylon chains are documented under the other-polymers branch of the case.

facts.label: Friction
facts.value: POM has a very low coefficient of friction and no 'grease needed' behaviour

c64.keyboard.switches.plunger-polymer.note: Which polymer each production run used is not something the sources pin down; POM and filled nylon were both routine. Acetal has a very low coefficient of friction and never develops the grease-seeking behaviour that nylon can.

c64.case.shield.foil.name: Aluminium foil
c64.case.shield.foil.description: Aluminium foil carried on a cardboard backing (catalogued as cardboard foil shields), slit and die-cut. Household foil is 0.016 mm and heavy-duty household foil 0.024 mm; this is not a semi-rugged grade but ordinary foil given stiffness by its backing. Its job is not to be a Faraday cage in the strict sense but simply to be a continuous, grounded-ish conductor over the board so the radiated field collapses.
c64.case.shield.foil.note: Corrected: the 0.03-0.06 mm gauge first stated here is heavier than either standard household foil (0.016 mm) or heavy-duty household foil (0.024 mm). The C64 shields are catalogued as cardboard foil shields, which reads as foil carried on a cardboard backing rather than bare foil, and later breadbin boards used a stamped metal shield and heatsink instead. Foil tears easily, so the practical difficulty of using it is handling, not the material.

c64.case.shield.spacer.name: Shield spacer (board core)
c64.case.shield.spacer.description: A rigidising core so the foil does not crumple and short against the board. Cheap versions use thin greyboard; better ones use a plastic-fibre or corrugated spacer. This is the part that makes the shield stand off the motherboard so it cannot touch solder joints.
c64.case.shield.spacer.note: Board core is a plausible choice because the shield only needs to hold a shape and take handling, and greyboard is the cheapest stiff sheet in existence. Stamped sheet-metal shields were the alternative on later boards.

c64.case.feet.elastomer.name: Foot elastomer compound
c64.case.feet.elastomer.description: A soft, low-durometer elastomer drop-in-moulded over a small ABS boss, or a moulded-in flexible nub. The chemistry is trivial but the tooling is not: it is a two-shot or insert-mould operation with an elastomer barrel and a much longer cure than the ABS.
c64.case.feet.elastomer.note: The chemistry is trivial but the tooling is not: this is a two-shot or insert-mould operation with an elastomer barrel and a much longer cure than the ABS. It reuses the same butadiene and styrene monomers as the ABS and the SBR, which is a reminder that all four plastics in this machine trace back to the same steam cracker.

c64.decor.prepress.film.name: Ortho photographic film (negative)
c64.decor.prepress.film.description: The black-and-white film that carries the image to the plate. It is a cellulose or polyester film coated with a silver-halide emulsion; exposed in a process camera or a contact frame, then developed and fixed in a chemical line.
c64.decor.prepress.film.note: Not established: the film type and gauge carried on a Commodore prepress line. The material is described here as a class of product, not a recorded part.

c64.decor.screen-print.mesh.name: Screen mesh (nylon monofilament or stainless wire)
c64.decor.screen-print.mesh.description: A woven mesh stretched and glued to an aluminium frame. Nylon is used where solvent or epoxy inks would attack a wire screen; stainless wire is used where long life under abrasive inks matters. Both are woven from a drawn filament or wire on a loom.

facts.label: Count
facts.value: ~100-200 mesh for fine legends, coarser for solid areas

c64.decor.screen-print.mesh.note: In part in conflict: the source says the most popular mesh in general use is made of polyester, with special-use mesh materials of nylon and stainless steel available to the screen-printer. That nylon and stainless are the special-case materials here is therefore the right shape of claim, but the 100-200 mesh count, the 50-80 um drawn filament and the aluminium frame are not established. The nylon is hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid again - the same PA6,6 that goes into connector latches, drawn down to 50-80 um for the mesh.

c64.decor.screen-print.emulsion.name: Screen emulsion (PVA or diazo)
c64.decor.screen-print.emulsion.description: The photosensitive coating that becomes the stencil. Diazo emulsions, standard in 1982, are washed out with water after exposure; PVA emulsion requires a separate exposure through the base and is more solvent-resistant. The stencil is exposed through a film positive and then washed.

facts.label: Common type (1982)
facts.value: diazo resin emulsion on mesh

facts.label: Stencil
facts.value: ~0.05-0.1 mm thick

c64.decor.screen-print.emulsion.note: Not established: whether the stencils were diazo or PVA emulsions, and the stencil thickness. Screen printing as such is documented; the specific chemistry on a Commodore line is not.

c64.decor.screen-print.ink.name: Screen-printing ink (one-part epoxy)
c64.decor.screen-print.ink.description: A one-component epoxy or polyester ink with a latent hardener, screen-printed through the stencil and then heat-cured. Epoxy ink is unusually durable on plastics and is what screen-printed Commodore product panels and keycap overlays used.
c64.decor.screen-print.ink.note: One-part epoxy inks cure at 120-150 C for 5-20 minutes, or flash to UV if the formulation is UV-curable. Epoxy ink is unusually durable on plastics and is what screen-printed Commodore product panels used; the epoxy chain from bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin is documented under the other-polymers branch of the case.

c64.decor.pad-print.pad.name: Silicone rubber printing pad
c64.decor.pad-print.pad.description: A soft, solvent-resistant, low-surface-energy pad, almost always silicone rubber, cut or cast with the relief to pick up and transfer the image. It is the consumable that has to be replaced every few thousand impressions, and pad hardness relative to the detail size is the operator's main variable.

facts.label: Hardness
facts.value: Shore A 30-70 depending on the image

facts.label: Life
facts.value: thousands to tens of thousands of impressions

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: two-part cast pad with a hardened steel or aluminium backing

c64.decor.pad-print.ink.name: Pad-printing ink (solvent or UV)
c64.decor.pad-print.ink.description: A free-flowing, low-viscosity ink that will transfer off a soft pad and then dry on a plastic part. In 1982 most pad inks were solvent-based (glycol ether / xylene / ester solvent with an alkyd or acrylic resin and a pigment); UV-curing pad inks existed and were gaining ground, and were faster but needed a lamp.

facts.label: Viscosity
facts.value: very low, ~10-40 s Zahn cup

facts.label: Drying
facts.value: air dry (minutes), heat (seconds), or UV (instant)

c64.decor.pad-print.ink.note: Not established: the solvent system, the resin and the viscosity of Commodore pad-printing ink, and whether the volume route in 1982 was solvent or UV. The general pad-printing mechanism is documented.

c64.packaging.litho-plate.name: Lithographic printing plate
c64.packaging.litho-plate.description: A thin aluminium or copper plate, grained and treated, with a photopolymer or metal-image layer carrying the separations. The classic long-run offset plate is an aluminium sheet electro-grained and anodised; short runs use photopolymer plates directly.

facts.label: Plate
facts.value: aluminium (offset), copper (letterpress), or photopolymer

c64.packaging.litho-plate.note: Not established: whether the plates were grained aluminium offset plates or photopolymer plates on the C64 packaging runs.

c64.packaging.litho-ink.name: Offset printing ink
c64.packaging.litho-ink.description: A pigment dispersed in a drying-oil-based vehicle (linseed/soy alkyd) with resin, wax and a drier. Water-based offset inks became the norm for corrugated in the 1990s; oil-based inks were standard in 1982.

facts.label: Vehicle
facts.value: linseed or soy alkyd resin

facts.label: Pigments
facts.value: titanium dioxide white, phthalocyanine blues, phthalochromate yellows

c64.case.tooling.chromium-acid.name: Chromic acid
c64.case.tooling.chromium-acid.description: Made by roasting chromite with soda ash and limestone, leaching the sodium chromate, and acidifying. So the chromium in the plating bath comes from the same chromite that came into the tool steel.

facts.label: Roasting
facts.value: about 1000 C with soda ash and lime, oxidative roast to Na2CrO4

facts.label: Acidification
facts.value: sulfuric acid to chromic acid

c64.case.tooling.chromium-acid.note: Not established: the roast temperature and the acidification route for the chromic acid in the plating bath, and that the plating bath chromium came from the same chromite as the tool steel.

c64.case.tooling.lapping-compound.name: Abrasive polishing compounds
c64.case.tooling.lapping-compound.description: Aluminium oxide for the bulk stock removal and green chromium oxide for the final mirror, both graded by grain size and applied on cloth and stone. This is the most labour-intensive step in the whole case tool: a large textured housing cavity takes days of hand polishing on cast-iron blocks, which is why such tools cost tens of thousands of dollars and why the economics demanded millions of parts.

facts.label: Media
facts.value: aluminium oxide for bulk, chromium oxide for the final mirror

facts.label: Final flat-surface finish
facts.value: Ra 0.05-0.1 um before plating

facts.label: Hand vs machine
facts.value: hand polishing on cast iron for the final mirror; machine polish for stock removal

c64.case.tooling.lapping-compound.note: Not established: the media grades, the finished roughness and the hand-polishing route used on the C64 case tools.

c64.case.tooling.graphite-electrode.name: Graphite electrode for EDM texturing
c64.case.tooling.graphite-electrode.description: Isostatic-pressed fine-grain graphite, turned or milled to the negative of the texture panel, or a CNC-shaped graphite block. Graphite is used because it is easy to machine, wears predictably as the electrode erodes, and does not damage the workpiece the way a metal electrode would.
c64.case.tooling.graphite-electrode.note: Not established: the isostatic pressing, the grade, and the claim that graphite does not damage the workpiece in a way a metal electrode would. That a shaped electrode is used at all is documented.

c64.case.tooling.brass-electrode.name: Brass electrode for fine detail
c64.case.tooling.brass-electrode.description: Copper-zinc alloy electrodes are used where the texture has fine features, because brass machines more accurately than graphite and can be reworked. Brass comes from copper and zinc ores smelted together.
c64.case.tooling.brass-electrode.note: Not established: that brass electrodes were used on the C64 case texture, and for which features. Electrodes and their relative behaviour are documented generally; the choice on this tool is not.

c64.packaging.digestion.name: Kraft cooking (digestion)
c64.packaging.digestion.description: Chips are cooked in a spherical or continuous digester with white liquor (sodium hydroxide + sodium sulfide + sodium carbonate) at 160-180 C. The alkali dissolves the lignin; the sulfide keeps the dissolved lignin in solution so the fibres do not darken.

facts.label: Duration
facts.value: 1-3 hours

facts.label: Chemical recovery
facts.value: black liquor is evaporated and burnt to regenerate the chemicals

c64.packaging.digestion.note: Not established: the cook temperature, the duration and the white-liquor composition, and that the digester sat next to a Commodore packaging supplier rather than a paper mill.

c64.packaging.kraft-process.name: Kraft grade versus bleached
c64.packaging.kraft-process.description: Unbleached kraft keeps its brown colour and is the cheapest strong liner; kraft paper is also known as brown paper. The colour is a property of the unbleached grade rather than of retained lignin, since the kraft cook removes most of the wood's lignin. A bleached or semi-bleached top liner costs more and is used where the print needs a white background. Commodore's boxes are brown board with printing on top, so the brown liner is exactly right.

facts.label: Bleaching
facts.value: chlorine, chlorine dioxide or oxygen/peroxide delignification

c64.packaging.kraft-process.note: That unbleached kraft is cheaper than a bleached top liner is established in general terms by kraft paper also being known as brown paper, and produced from the kraft process. Not established: that the pulp is brown before it reaches the paper machine because the cook keeps the lignin, since the source says kraft pulping removes most of the lignin; the bleaching chemistries; or that Commodore's boxes were brown board with printing on top. Chlorine bleaching of pulp was standard in 1982 and has since been largely displaced by chlorine-free processes for environmental reasons - a clear 1980s-versus-modern difference in the same plant.

c64.case.abs-resin.c8-aromatics-separati.name: C8 aromatics separation (UOP Parex)
c64.case.abs-resin.c8-aromatics-separati.description: Para-xylene is selectively adsorbed from the mixed C8 aromatics onto a zeolite molecular sieve, desorbed with a purge, leaving o- and m-xylene. It is a swinging adsorption unit with hundreds of adsorbent beds and rotating valves.

facts.label: Sorbent
facts.value: X/Y zeolite molecular sieve

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: ~96-99% para-xylene recovery

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: mixed C8 aromatics from the reformer

c64.case.abs-resin.c8-aromatics-separati.note: Not established: the sorbent grade, the number of beds and the 96-99% para-xylene recovery figure, and that a 1982 ABS supplier used a Parex unit at all. No encyclopaedia article covers the Parex process, and the C64 own documents say nothing about the petrochemical chain feeding the resin.

c64.packaging.eps-expansion.name: Bead expansion (bead expander)
c64.packaging.eps-expansion.description: Beads are fed into a steam-heated expander where they expand, are held at temperature to sinter them into a cake, and are then cooled and dried in a silo. The expander is the machine that sets the final foam density.

facts.label: Expansion ratio
facts.value: about 50-100x by volume

c64.packaging.eps-expansion.note: Not established: the expansion ratio and the expander used on the Commodore packing line.

c64.packaging.eps-moulding.name: Block moulding in a steam-heated mould
c64.packaging.eps-moulding.description: Beads are blown into a heated aluminium mould and the steam expands them to fill it; the mould is then cooled and the block ejected. A block mould makes a slab that is later cut on a band saw or hot wire into the end blocks. The mould is a heat exchanger - the steam lines run through it.

facts.label: Mould
facts.value: steam-heated aluminium, 100-140 C; cycle about 1-3 minutes

c64.packaging.eps-moulding.note: Not established: the mould temperature, the cycle time and that the C64 end blocks were cut from a block mould.

c64.packaging.deinking.name: Repulping and deinking
c64.packaging.deinking.description: Bales are dropped into a hydrapulper, torn up into fibre, screened, and deinked with a flotation cell and surfactant to remove printing inks. A high proportion of the world's corrugated medium fibre is recovered in exactly this way.
c64.packaging.deinking.note: That deinking is the named industrial process for removing printing ink from paper fibres to make deinked pulp is established. Not established: the hydrapulper and flotation-cell sequence, the caustic and surfactant charges, and that a high proportion of the world's corrugated medium fibre is recovered this way.

c64.cables.rf-cable.copper-wire.name: Copper wire rod and drawing
c64.cables.rf-cable.copper-wire.description: Copper cathodes are melted, cast into wire rod, then drawn through a series of dies to the finished diameter. A cable plant buys rod and draws it in-house; drawing anneals and work-hardens the copper in the same step.

facts.label: Copper purity
facts.value: E-C grade 99.9%+, from electrolytic refining

facts.label: Drawing
facts.value: wet or dry, through carbide or diamond dies

c64.cables.rf-cable.copper-wire.note: Not established: the purity grade, the die material and whether the C64 cable plant drew wire in house.

c64.decor.pad-print.electroplating.name: Copper electrotyping the plate
c64.decor.pad-print.electroplating.description: The sensitised copper plate is electroplated in an acid copper bath to build a thick deposit on the image, then the surface is ground and polished back so only the image stands proud. It is an old, slow process, but it gives an image hard enough to print millions of impressions.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: acidified copper sulphate with an additive

c64.decor.pad-print.electroplating.note: Not established: that Commodore printing plates were copper electrotypes, and the deposit thickness and bath conditions. Electrotyping is an old process but no Commodore record of it has been found.

c64.packaging.film-blowing.name: Film blowing and bag making
c64.packaging.film-blowing.description: LDPE pellets are blown as a thin tube through a die and a bubble, cooled in an air ring, collapsed and wound; the tube is then cut and heat-sealed into a bag. Film blowing is high-volume and very cheap - the bag is cents, not dollars.

facts.label: Line speed
facts.value: 100+ m/min of collapsed tube

c64.packaging.film-blowing.note: Not established: the film gauge and line speed. Film blowing is a documented process; that it made this bag is not.

c64.packaging.manual.printing.name: Colour offset printing of the manual
c64.packaging.manual.printing.description: Sheet-fed offset litho in four colours (CMYK), plus spot colours for the Commodore rainbow and the red 'RESTORE' key highlights. The manual's diagrams and BASIC listings were set in hot-metal or phototypeset, then printed from plates.

facts.label: Colours
facts.value: process CMYK plus spot colours

facts.label: Prepress
facts.value: phototypesetting and photographic copy for the diagrams

c64.packaging.manual.printing.note: Not established: the press type, the colour count and the spot colours on the C64 manual. The manual as a part is documented; how it was printed is not.

c64.packaging.box-printing.name: Box printing (offset litho) and the rainbow graphics
c64.packaging.box-printing.description: The printed sheet is run on an offset litho press - sheet-fed for short runs, web-fed for long - in a small number of process colours, with the Commodore rainbow reproduced as a multi-stop gradient from duotone overprints at varying screen densities or, on later short runs, a spray unit. A thin aqueous varnish is often applied over the top for scuff resistance. Flexographic printing on corrugate with rubber or photopolymer plates became the normal route for high-run corrugated print during this period and later; for a mid-run consumer box in the early 1980s, sheet-fed offset on a liner was still common.

facts.label: Press
facts.value: sheet-fed offset or rotary web offset

facts.label: Colours
facts.value: typically 3-6 process colours; the rainbow needs extra separations or a duotone gradient

facts.label: Surface
facts.value: uncoated kraft board, often with a thin aqueous varnish

c64.packaging.box-printing.note: The offset mechanism is established: the inked image is transferred from a plate to a rubber blanket and then to the printing surface, with a water roller applying a water-based film to the non-image areas. Not established: that the Commodore rainbow on the box was run on an offset press at all, that it was reproduced as a duotone gradient from overprints at varying screen densities or on a spray unit, the three-to-six process colour count, and the aqueous varnish. The number of separations and the duotone-versus-spray choice vary by printing run and region; the visual effect, a rainbow gradient band, is consistent across the packaging.

children.name: Offset lithographic printing
children.description: The image is on a flat plate, wetted with dampening solution so the image areas reject ink, and printed by a rubber blanket onto paper. Litho gives fine detail and consistent colour on uncoated board, at the cost of a plate-making step per colour.

facts.label: Process colours
facts.value: cyan, magenta, yellow, black (CMYK)

facts.label: Press
facts.value: sheet-fed or web-fed

children.name: Offset press (sheet-fed or web)
children.description: A printing press: plate cylinders, blanket cylinders, inking units, and either a sheet feed with a delivery stacker or a web unwind and rewind with a folder. For a corrugated box liner, the press is the capital equipment a converter owns.

facts.label: Units
facts.value: 2-6 inking units for up to 6 colours

children.note: Not established: the press type, the unit count and the frame. Offset printing is documented; the machine that printed Commodore packaging is not identified.

c64.keyboard.keycaps.legend.name: Printed front (PETSCII) legends
c64.keyboard.keycaps.legend.description: The graphics characters on the small FRONT wall of the cap - the PETSCII and shifted-symbol set - are printed, not moulded. This is the other half of the keycap story from the double-shot top legends (c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot), and the difference is visible: these characters wear and rub off, so a cap whose front legend is faint while its top legend is crisp is normal rather than damaged. Printing a near-vertical face is harder than printing a top - the pad has to be tilted against the front wall with the cap held in a nest, which wants a second station and a second fixture - so front coverage improves gradually across a production run rather than switching on at a date. On sets with only a single top legend, the front face was left plain.

facts.label: Applies to
facts.value: the front wall only - PETSCII and shifted graphics characters

facts.label: Process
facts.value: printed; the sources say pad printing but hedge it ("likely pad-printed")

facts.label: Wear
facts.value: yes - these are the legends that rub off, unlike the moulded tops

facts.label: Why a vertical face is harder
facts.value: the pad must be tilted against the front wall with the cap held in a nest

facts.label: Front-face coverage
facts.value: improves gradually across the production run rather than switching on at a date

c64.keyboard.keycaps.legend.note: The front legends are printed and the cap tops are not: this node covers the front wall only. The 1982 breadbin keycap is double-shot moulded on top (see c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot) and printed on the front. Evidence: Keyboard Wiki (themk.org) - "The front-printed "PETSCII" legends are likely pad-printed"; Deskthority 8102 - "The front legends are printed. If you look closely you should see the difference between double shot on the top and printed on the front of the caps." Confidence is held at medium for a specific reason: that the front legends are PRINTED is well attested by two independent collector sources, but the sources do not agree on the method - the Keyboard Wiki hedges with "likely" while Deskthority only says "printed". The ink and pad-printing detail retained here follows the pad-printing reading and should be treated as the weaker half of this node.

c64.case.moulding.name: Injection moulding of the case
c64.case.moulding.description: The bezel and rear shell are moulded on a large toggle or hydraulic press in a multi-cavity family tool. Dried ABS is melted in a three- or four-zone barrel at 200-260 C, injected through a gate on the parting line at 1000-1500 bar, packed at 50-100 bar until the gate freezes, cooled against water channels at 40-60 C until the part has shrunk onto the tool, and pushed off the core on ejector pins that leave small round marks and a gate vestige on the seam. Because ABS shrinks 0.4-0.7% linearly the tool is cut oversize, and because the wall is only 2.5-3.5 mm the melt has to snake a long, thin, textured flow in under a second or it cools and frosts. That combination is why C64 cases carry visible flow marks: the two-point pattern is the frozen boundary where two melt fronts met and did not fully knit.

facts.label: Press clamp force
facts.value: 300-600 t (the C64 case is a wide but shallow tool)

facts.label: Melt temperature
facts.value: 230-260 C; barrel zones about 200 / 230 / 245 / 250 C

facts.label: Mould temperature
facts.value: 40-60 C, water-jacketed

facts.label: Pack pressure
facts.value: 50-100 bar, held while the gate freezes

facts.label: Cooling time
facts.value: 20-40 s, the dominant term in the cycle

facts.label: Cycle time
facts.value: 30-60 s for a case this size

facts.label: ABS shrinkage
facts.value: 0.4-0.7% linear, so the cavity is cut oversize

facts.label: Ejector pin mark
facts.value: about 3-6 mm diameter, faint circular imprint

facts.label: Screw residence time
facts.value: keep under about 10 min to avoid thermal degradation

c64.case.moulding.note: Not established: the clamp force, the melt and mould temperatures, the injection and pack pressures, the cooling time, the cycle time and the wall thickness on a Commodore breadbin tool. The general sequence of injection moulding is documented; none of these figures is.

children.name: Injection press (300-600 t)
children.description: A toggle or direct-hydraulic injection moulding machine with a screw plasticiser, a heated barrel with three or four zones, an oil or water temperature controller, and a mould base. Toggle machines clamp faster and are what most housing tools ran on. Oil hydraulics drive the toggle or the platen, provide injection and holding pressure, and drive the ejector; hydraulic pressure is the reason injection pressure reached 1000-1500 bar, against the about 500 bar of the older toggle-and-screw machines.

children.name: Plasticising screw and barrel
children.description: A flighted screw turns in a heated barrel, conveying and melting pellets on the way back and injecting on the way forward. The screw is nitrided 33CrMoV or 40Cr steel, bimetallic-lined at the tip in later designs.

facts.label: Diameter
facts.value: typically 25-40 mm L/D 20-28 for this shot size

facts.label: Screw material
facts.value: nitrided 33CrMoV, or bimetallic barrel

children.note: Not established: the screw diameter, the L/D ratio and the nitrided grade on the C64 case press. The general function of a plasticising screw is documented.

children.name: Hydraulic clamp unit
children.description: Oil hydraulics drive the toggle or the platen, provide injection and holding pressure, and drive the ejector. A hydraulic press is the reason injection pressure reached 1000+ bar - compared with the ~500 bar of the older toggle-and-screw machines.

facts.label: Oil
facts.value: hydraulic oil, ISO VG 46-68

children.note: Not established: the injection pressures, the oil grade and the clamp force on a C64 case press.

facts.label: Screw
facts.value: nitrided 33CrMoV or bimetallic-lined, 25-40 mm diameter at L/D 20-28

facts.label: Hydraulic oil
facts.value: ISO VG 46-68

children.note: Not established: the clamp force, the screw diameter and ratio, the barrel zoning and the hydraulic oil grade on the press that moulded the case.

c64.cables.rf-cable.polymer-extrusion.name: Cable extrusion line
c64.cables.rf-cable.polymer-extrusion.description: A vertical or horizontal line where conductor is drawn through a die, dielectric tube is extruded or foamed around it, braid is laid on from a rotating carrier, and the jacket is extruded and cooled in a trough. Cable extrusion is one of the few polymer processes that is genuinely continuous and high-speed.

facts.label: Line speed
facts.value: tens to hundreds of m/min

facts.label: Steps
facts.value: conductor -> dielectric -> braid -> jacket, often on separate lines

facts.label: Spark testing
facts.value: each length passes a high-voltage spark tester

c64.cables.rf-cable.polymer-extrusion.note: Not established: the line speed, the number of passes and the spark test on the cable that shipped with the C64.

c64.keyboard.keycaps.tool.name: Keycap tool (small multi-cavity, hardened steel)
c64.keyboard.keycaps.tool.description: Keycaps are made in small high-cavity tools - 4, 8 or 16 cavities in one block - because a cap is cheap and the tool has to be small enough to fit a small press. The tool is hardened tool steel and the caps come off a common gate, so the visible faces are identical across the set. A cap is the shortest flow in moulding: a shallow thin-walled box filled through a single gate, which is why the tool is small, multi-cavity and warm-moulded, and why the cycle is 15-30 s against 30-60 s for a case.

facts.label: Tool size
facts.value: about 150 x 150 mm

facts.label: Tool life
facts.value: 300,000-1,000,000 shots, replated and repolished on rebuild

facts.label: Fill time
facts.value: under 1 s through a single gate on the inside wall

c64.keyboard.keycaps.tool.note: Not established: the cavity count, the tool size, the cycle time and the tool life on a Commodore keycap tool.

c64.case.tooling.name: Case tooling: H13 family mould with EDM texture
c64.case.tooling.description: The two breadbin case moulds are large two-plate tools in pre-hardened or hardened hot-work steel, with the leather-grain texture cut by electrical discharge machining and the cavity polished and hard-chromed. A single mould produces thousands of C64 cases; its cost is amortised over millions of parts, so Commodore could afford a 5-cavity family tool.

facts.label: Tool size
facts.value: ~450 x 350 mm, two-plate, guided by leader pins

facts.label: Cavities
facts.value: typically 1 large cavity for a case this size; 2-4 on smaller tools

facts.label: Tool life for ABS housing
facts.value: 300,000-1,000,000 shots before re-polish or repair

facts.label: Nickel content of plating
facts.value: hard chrome, or electroless nickel of ~5-10 um

facts.label: Tool life by run size
facts.value: large ABS housing tool 300,000-1,000,000+ shots with periodic rebuild; small high-cavity keycap tool similar; short-run and prototype tools may only see 30,000-200,000

c64.case.tooling.note: Not established: the tool size, the cavity count, the plating thickness and the tool life on the two Commodore breadbin case tools.

children.name: Mould assembly: guide pins, ejectors, cooling
children.description: The finished plates are set into a mould base with guide pillars or bushes, an ejector-plate assembly with pins under every feature that would imprint on the visible face, and water lines carrying coolant through the cores and plates to remove the heat of plasticisation.

facts.label: Guide elements
facts.value: 4 large guide pillars with bushings

facts.label: Ejector pins
facts.value: hardened, nitrided, about 3-6 mm diameter

facts.label: Cooling
facts.value: water at 30-60 C through baffles and core channels

facts.label: Hot runner
facts.value: unusual on a large ABS housing tool in 1982; cold runner with a pressure-controlled gate was normal

children.note: Not established: the guide pillar count, the ejector pin diameter, the coolant temperature and the cold-runner choice on a Commodore case tool.

c64.packaging.packaging-line.name: Pack-out and case packing
c64.packaging.packaging-line.description: At the end of the case-moulding and assembly plant, machines are bagged, placed in the foam blocks, dropped into the printed box with the manual and the warranty card, and the box is closed, labelled and case-packed. This was semi-automatic and was the labour-heavy step that determined where a home computer was finally assembled.

facts.label: Operations
facts.value: bag, foam, box, insert paper, close, label, case-pack

facts.label: Labour
facts.value: a few operators per line; the constraint on Commodore's throughput

c64.packaging.packaging-line.note: Not established: the operations, the operator count and where pack-out was done. A C64 box, foam end blocks and a printed manual are documented by the parts list; the pack-out line that combined them is not.

c64.decor.pad-printing.name: Pad printing the legends and badge
c64.decor.pad-printing.description: The workhorse decorating process on this machine. A soft silicone rubber pad is pressed onto a flat metal cliche carrying the image in wet ink, picks the ink up on its raised relief, then deforms against the curved or textured plastic part and transfers the image. One pad, one colour, one station; two stations give the two-colour keycap legends. It is chosen over screen printing precisely because the parts are curved, crowned and leather-grained, none of which a flat screen will lie against.

facts.label: Stations
facts.value: 1-2 (single or two-colour)

facts.label: Throughput
facts.value: hundreds to thousands of impressions per hour

facts.label: Surface tolerance
facts.value: curved, crowned and textured parts, unlike screen printing

facts.label: Inspection
facts.value: 100% visual under a fixed lamp; registration to a fraction of a character width

children.name: Two-colour pad printing press
children.description: A small cast frame with a plate table, an ink cup or doctor blade, a silicone pad on a shuttle head, and part fixtures on a rotating or indexing table. Each colour station is one table position with its own pad.

facts.label: Configuration
facts.value: indexing table with 2-8 stations

children.note: Not established: the station count, the index table and the registration tolerance on a Commodore decorating line. Pad printing presses are described in the general literature; a Commodore one is not identified.

children.name: Cliche (printing plate)
children.description: The flat copper or nickel electrotype that carries the image, sunk into a plate table and flooded with ink. The traditional route photographs the artwork onto a sensitised copper plate, electroplates it up to about 1 mm and then grinds and polishes the surface back so that only the image stands proud; the photopolymer plate is the same object made from a photosensitive polymer film on a steel backing, exposed through the artwork film and washed out in relief, which needs no electroplating step and suits short runs. A flat pad-print cliche is a simpler object than a litho plate because there is no water damping - it is essentially a stencil on a copper block - which is why pad printing was chosen for short runs as well as long ones.

facts.label: Plate
facts.value: copper or nickel electrotype, or a photopolymer plate on a steel backing

facts.label: Image relief
facts.value: about 0.05-0.2 mm on an electrotype, 0.1-0.5 mm on a photopolymer

facts.label: Electrodeposit
facts.value: about 1 mm, ground and polished back to the relief

children.note: That the plate carrying the image in pad printing is called a cliche is established by the process description, which names the cliche as the element the image is transferred from via the silicone pad. Not established: which of the two routes Commodore used, and it does not change what the cliche is - a copper electrotype with a ground-back relief, or a photopolymer plate on a steel backing. The electrotype is the older route and the one a print shop could repair; the photopolymer plate is cheaper per plate and better on fine detail, which matters for a 66-character legend set.

children.name: UV curing of ink
children.description: A mercury or metal-halide lamp floods the printed part in under a second and the photo-initiator in the ink polymerises it in place. It was the big printing-technology change of the late 1970s and early 1980s: instant cure, no solvent, no oven, and a harder, more abrasion-resistant print.

facts.label: Lamp
facts.value: medium-pressure mercury, 80-120 W/cm

facts.label: Cure time
facts.value: sub-second per exposure

facts.label: Photo-initiator
facts.value: a benzophenone or imidazole ketone

children.note: Two elements are established: the photoinitiator is what absorbs the light and starts the reaction, which controls the cure rate and depth of cure; and medium-pressure mercury-vapor lamps have historically been the industry standard for curing products with ultraviolet light. Not established: the 80-120 W/cm lamp rating, the sub-second cure, that the photo-initiator was a benzophenone or an imidazole ketone, and that UV was established on Commodore keycaps by 1982 while solvent drying was still the volume route. By 1982 UV curing was established in screen and pad printing on plastics but not yet universal; solvent drying was still the volume route. Its big advantage for a decorating shop is that a printed keycap can be stacked immediately with no drying time.

c64.decor.pad-printing.note: Registration is the skill of the job: on a two-colour legend the second impression has to land exactly on top of the first, shifted symbols and all, so every printed part is checked for legibility, registration and offset before it goes into the machine, under a fixed lamp. A shift of half a character width is a reject, which is one reason the legends look so consistent on surviving machines. UV-curing ink was available by 1982 and needed no drying time, but solvent drying was still the volume route.

c64.decor.screen-printing.name: Screen printing
c64.decor.screen-printing.description: Silk screening through a mesh, used on Commodore parts where the surface is flat enough: printed panels, cartridge labels and some case markings. It cannot print the grain-textured bezel reliably, which is exactly why pad printing won on the case and on the keycaps.

facts.label: Mesh
facts.value: nylon monofilament or stainless steel wire, 100-200 mesh

children.name: Squeegee blade
children.description: A rubber or neoprene blade in a wooden or aluminium holder that forces ink through the stencil and wipes the surface. The durometer of the blade is the operator's variable: hard for fine detail, soft for heavy coverage.

c64.decor.screen-printing.note: Retained because Commodore did screen-print product panels and cartridge labels, but nothing on the breadbin case or keycaps went through a screen.

c64.decor.prepress.name: Prepress: artwork to film and plate
c64.decor.prepress.description: Every legend and every logo started as artwork, composed mechanically or photographically in 1982, then copied onto black-and-white film by a process camera; the film was used to expose a plate, either a photopolymer or an electrotyped copper one. Text was set in hot metal or phototype, and the Commodore rainbow artwork was assembled from hand-painted separations.

facts.label: Text setting
facts.value: hot metal or phototypesetting, later CRT phototype

facts.label: Copy
facts.value: process camera onto ortho film

facts.label: Plates
facts.value: photopolymer, or electrotyped copper

c64.decor.prepress.note: Not established: which of the two plate routes Commodore used, and how the rainbow separations were made. The camera-to-film-to-plate sequence is a printing-industry convention rather than a documented Commodore practice.

c64.decor.metallised.name: Metallised and pearlescent ink
c64.decor.metallised.description: The shiny bars in the Commodore rainbow badge are metallised ink: pigment-grade aluminium flake suspended in a binder and printed, then optionally burnished between heated polished rollers so the flakes lie flat and mirror rather than scatter. The same effect could be had from a hot foil, pressed from vacuum-metallised polyester or aluminium film with a type plate, but on a textured ABS case the foil needs a rougher surface or a soft die, which is why flake ink won.

facts.label: Flake
facts.value: atomised aluminium, about 5-15 um

facts.label: Alternative route
facts.value: hot foil stamping, 150-250 C die; lost to flake ink on a textured case

facts.label: Appearance
facts.value: burnished flake reads as a flat mirror-like metallic that shifts with viewing angle

c64.decor.metallised.note: Not established: that the Commodore rainbow badge was printed in metallised flake ink, and that the print was burnished. The comparison against hot foil stamping is a general decorating argument, not a record of what Commodore did.
